en: Preface to the Re-engraved *Western Regions Synthesis* (*Xifang helun*).
Confucians establish heaven and earth and rectify the human form through the Three Bonds and Five Constants;

yet, when it comes to severing birth and death and emerging from the mundane world, one must rely upon Buddhism. Among the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, Amitābha is foremost.
First, among the various pure lands each Buddha presides over, the Western World of Ultimate Bliss is foremost.

Among the infinite methods of practice and contemplative gates for seeking rebirth in the pure land through the recitation of the Buddha’s name, single-mindedly holding the Name without distraction is foremost.
Throughout antiquity and the present, the sages and worthies have praised the teaching of the Pure Land and the practice of nianfo as being like heaven itself.

The *Ten Doubts on the Pure Land* (Tai shi yi lun) by Yongming, the *Wanxian Tonggui* (Myriad Good Deeds Return to One Source), and Tianru’s *Or-wen Longshu Jingtu wen* (Questions and Answers on the Pure Land Texts of Longshu) have already provided detailed explanations;
however, their meanings are scattered across various volumes and housed in separate cases.

Subsequently, the *Amitābha Sūtra Commentary* (Mituo shuchao) by the Great Master Yunqi of the Ming Dynasty synthesized these into a grand compendium. Furthermore, there was Mr. Yuan Shigong, styled Hongdao, from Gong’an in Hubei.
This work, the *Xi-fang-he-lun* (Treatise on the Convergence of the West), reconciles differences, resolves doubts and obstructions, and elucidates the profound mysteries;
it directly points toward the ultimate goal and takes the Buddhist scriptures as its primary warp, while his elder brother raises them up and his younger brother propagates them.

Truly, they are the Vasubandhu and Asaṅga of the Confucian tradition, and the Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna of the treatise schools—truly those who manifested in the bodies of officials and laymen to spread the Dharma.
This encompasses the practices of co-residence and co-practice; when the practice of nianfo reaches this stage, it truly constitutes the Pure Land of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Only upon reaching this may one be called a practitioner who has realized the principle that "all is mind. It is fitting for every person to keep a copy of this work at hand and read it several times each day.

Although the commentaries and sub-commentaries have already circulated widely in the world, the *He lun* (Compendium) is rarely recognized by those who encounter its text. Now, the Dharma is declining and the kalpa of calamity is just beginning.

The fourfold assembly of this Sahā world should quickly aspire to be reborn there; yet, they are not free from divergent paths in doctrine and religious practice, nor do they lack doubts regarding Chan and Pure Land.
Thus, the lotus flower may suddenly bloom or wither, and the Pure Land may seem near or far.
It is for these reasons that Amitābha Buddha, moved by profound compassion and urgent necessity, has employed his broad and long tongue through the writings of Yuan to cry out in distress.

I, Ye Kui, have long received the Buddha’s grace; though I am mired and obstructed within this turbid world, I take refuge in this Way. Desiring to propagate this book, I found my strength insufficient.

Happily, there were two lay practitioners and fellow seekers of the Way—Gan Er (style name Youmin) and his younger brother, Gan Ceng (style name Zuomin)—who shared the same aspiration for Pure Land practice.
Upon seeing the *Dahe lun* (Great Harmony Treatise), they felt great satisfaction in their hearts and joyfully praised it, whereupon...

He contributed funds to have the woodblocks carved, joining with others to complete this work, so that the "Water-Moon" of the Yuan family may shine brightly once more and the "Flowers and Fruits" of the Lotus Pond may spread universally.
That every person who recites the Buddha's name sees the Buddha depends upon encountering this book;
that every person gains strength from this book depends upon this new carving. May one more person be born in the Pure Land, turning back to serve as my own companion.
The Master attains the realization of non-arising one day earlier than others, thereby ensuring the long-term continuation of the Buddha’s wisdom-life.
All who are loyal ministers, filial sons, righteous husbands, and chaste wives, as well as even the smallest crawling insects and flying creatures, are companions for the Land of Bliss.

All practices—whether meditating on Chan, reciting mantras, observing precepts, cultivating merit, or engaging in worldly affairs and daily labors—are provisions for rebirth there. Even a single instance of being encouraged to recite [the name] with stillness...
To spend one hour expounding a single word for its circulation in a single place is a matter of immeasurable merit and longevity;
it is the true reality of principle and fact, neither deceptive nor false. It is the equality of the Buddhas of past and present, neither easy nor difficult. The Pure Land is before my very eyes;
for those who possess the great vow, a single thought is sufficient—truly, nothing can surpass this!
Written on the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the year Dayuanyuan (1737), by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Zhou Zhikui of Min,
who bows his head;
recorded by the Master of Jingiang Pavilion, Gan Eryi.
The Yuan family’s devotion to the Pure Land was proven by the efficacy of their dream;
when I read the collected works of Master Zhonglang, I found that whenever news arrived regarding his family, he would join his palms and recite with praise:

"I have heard that my lord and all his kin have turned their hearts toward the pure karma—this is the foremost rare event in the human realm. What difficulty is there in single-mindedly upholding the Name?"
Yet people naturally harbor doubts and resistance; for such great wealth and honor, Heaven itself is unwilling to bestow them lightly upon anyone.
Furthermore, one must resolutely practice the Dharma to benefit and save others, and through patience, break down the marks of self and other, stinginess, and greed.
To become a sage or a Buddha is the most urgent of matters—this is the excellent medicine for those who today calculate every ounce and grain. Master.

The reason I have alone, within my dreams, diligently applied skillful means to compassionately exhort all beings without ceasing is that if one reads this compilation and does not feel a sense of sorrowful reflection and resolve, how could that be human nature? Recently, Mr.

Zhou Zhangfu pointed out the path of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation), and Yuanzi’s *Heli lun* (Comprehensive Discussion) exhaustively covers it; I have also recorded my dream to serve as an appendix to this *Heli lun*.

Only after the contract was concluded was I able to obtain this book to read; my younger brother Sīn and my son Yòu, while suffering from illness, heard its teachings and both conceived faith in them.
Consequently, I have entrusted it to the press for re-carving so as to encourage one another, and thus inform the wise and venerable elders.
If you consider me to be like one who offers the heat of summer when it is cold, I am deeply ashamed, deeply ashamed.

In the preface to the *Western Pure Land Synthesis* (*Xifang helun*), Master Xiangguang describes how, while he was cultivating pure practices in the seclusion of Xiaoshan Monastery, a certain Chan practitioner passed by his dwelling with a wide gaze and stately stride.
Upon seeing a book on the table, he read that it was the newly composed *Synthesis of Pure Land Teachings* (*Jingtu helun*) by the layman Shitou; however, he had not yet finished reading it.
The Master raised his voice and declared: "If we discuss this Dharma-gate, it was originally intended to guide those of middling and inferior faculties. Why is this?

Because those of middling and inferior faculties possess slight wisdom while the power of their karma is profound and vast; yet by recollecting the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, they attain birth in the Pure Land.
It is like a heavy stone attached to a boat that can reach the shore; one should truly practice mindfulness of the Buddha. As for us who have entered the Caves..."
When you realize the source, this very mind is the Buddha; where else could you seek the Buddha? This very mind is the Land; where else could you see the Land?
Within the reality of ultimate truth (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single hair’s breadth of the marks of birth and death, coming and going, or the three periods of time can be found.
To say one "attains Buddhahood" is already a superfluous expression; how could there be any further distinctions?

Regarding the matters of abandoning the pure and the defiled to be born in another realm: if one realizes here that one is a free and independent person, then lust, anger, and ignorance are all the equal Dharma-assembly of Amitābha;
they are suchness, immovable. Why then do you abandon your own Buddha to prostrate before that bronze image?
Furthermore, to claim that both the awakened and the unawakened should practice [this] is to create trouble where there is none.

"What I do not understand," Xiangguang heard this and sighed deeply, saying, "If what you say is merely intended to make your speech smooth and clever, you do not realize that with a single step you will fall into a pit of fire. Birth and death are impermanent;
they arrive in the blink of an eye. How can you take the ready-made, conventional phrases of the ancestral school as the ultimate, and simply say, 'I...'"?

Once one has already attained Buddhahood, there is no need to further recollect the Buddha. Speaking from the perspective of ultimate principle (*tattva*), every single speck of dust and every louse in the world possesses the Tathāgata’s pure body of awakening, which is non-dual and without distinction.
Even when all Buddhas have attained equal and perfect enlightenment and realized great *nirvāṇa*, their fundamental essence has never increased by so much as a single fraction;
likewise, when sentient beings fall into the three miserable realms or rush toward the ocean of birth and death, that essence has never diminished.
The fundamental essence has never diminished by even a single fraction; the body of suchness is eternally unmoving.

Birth-and-death and nirvana are but false perceptions; there is neither Tathāgata nor sentient being. Entering realization here, there is no person who realizes, nor is there any dharma that is realized.
When the scope of the mind is extinguished and severed, one transcends the realm of phenomena (*qing*), and upon the great earth, not a single inch remains.
Where shall the single word "earth-Buddha" be placed? Only when one enters the Dharma-gate of cultivation can one cultivate and realize within non-cultivation and non-realization;

yet, within this state beyond grades, there are thousands of differences in rank. Even if one reaches the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*Samyak-sambodhi*), one still does not know where the Tathāgata lifts his foot or sets it down.
This is why the ancestral masters of old reviled the Buddhas and rejected the teachings.

All these negations are intended to stop people from becoming attached to the characteristics of the teachings and developing interpretations based merely on the literal words, thereby failing to realize the fundamental essence beyond words.
They prevent one from dogmatically clinging to the provisional means within the words—whether it be speaking of mind, nature, emptiness, or illusion;
whether sudden or gradual; or cause and effect—yet they ensure that one thoroughly understands all the thousands of sutras and myriad treatises. When you question them...
Regarding one's own original life-spirit (*mūla-āyus*), one merely uses the ready-made words of the sutras and treatises to offer a rebuttal;

yet, once those ready-made words are set aside, one remains as before, utterly bewildered and at a loss. This is what is meant by "counting another's treasures while having not a single coin of one's own.

Even if there are practitioners of true cultivation who do not perceive their Buddha-nature and laboriously practice without a guide—like the blind—they will only obtain the status of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

The fruit of Heaven does not arise within the family of the Tathāgata. Thereupon, the patriarchs, perceiving this degeneration, employed their "poisonous hands" to eradicate his verbal expressions, block his paths of intellectual understanding, and press upon his conscious mind, compelling him to engage in arduous investigation and secret inquiry.

When the flow of birth and death and the emotions of birth and death were exhausted, and the thoughts of acceptance and rejection became empty, he finally recognized his own biological parents throughout kalpas.
The Treasure Store, however, examines the sutras and teachings one by one as matters within the house of the Way;
thereafter, he practices and cultivates according to what is taught, purifying residual habits with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

He pays homage to Tathāgatas who are like flowers in the sky, cultivates Brahma-conduct that is like the moon reflected in water, ascends the stages that are like a mirage, and delivers sentient beings who are like echoes in a valley. Without grasping at the realization of quiescence, this is called a Buddha.
The nature of the seeds is like the bright sun in the sky traveling upon the Great King’s road; it is not like wandering through the long night, crawling over thorns and falling into brambles.

Is it not said that after a single awakening, one immediately becomes identical to the ultimate fruit? When the Official (Fenggong) asked Master Cen Da-chong, "Is the Nirvana of the Fruit realized by the Good Knowledgeable Ones (Kalyāṇamitra) in the world?
Cen replied, "It is not yet realized. The Official asked, "Why is it not yet realized? Cen said: [The following text follows].
[The interlocutor] said: "If their merit is not yet equal to that of the various sages, how can they be called 'good spiritual friends' (kalyāṇamitra)? Cen said:
"One who clearly perceives the Buddha-nature may also be called a good spiritual friend. Chan Master Hongbian said:

"Although one suddenly realizes that one's own nature is identical to that of the Buddhas, because of the defiled habits accumulated since beginningless time, one must rely on remedial practices (*pratipakṣa*) to cause the functioning of the nature to arise in accordance with it."

It is like a person eating rice; they are not satisfied after just one mouthful. Guishan said, "When those with a beginner's mind attain sudden awakening to the fundamental principle through conditions, there still remain the habitual tendencies from beginningless, vast eons that cannot be suddenly purified. One must teach them to cleanse the flowing consciousness of present karma;
this is cultivation. It is not that there is some other separate dharma to teach them for their practice and progress. As for the various ancestral teachers..."

When one acts as a person, standing like a wall ten thousand fathoms high, within a great mass of fire where contact causes immediate burning, or amidst a forest of sword-trees where movement results in being consumed—before a word is even uttered, one is already separated by thousands and tens of thousands of miles.

Beyond such karmic conditions, when discussing the fundamental reality, the stages of practice have never been exhausted; they are clearly and in detail explained within the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp).

The instructions from the Great Wisdom Master Zhongfeng were especially urgent and earnest; he exhorted us with sincere devotion, fearing that people might cling to empty understanding and fall into demonic affairs.
He never once said that after a single awakening, one need not rely on cultivation, or that one would suddenly become equal to the Honored One with Two Feet and fully realize the fruit of Nirvana.
Later generations, failing to recognize the intent of his teachings and failing to grasp the mechanism of the Patriarchs, instead took...

To revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs, taking perilous phrases as one's practice—those of the past were hindered by sutras and treatises, which was like eating a mixture of rice and wheat that could not be properly digested;

those of later times are satiated with the memorization of Chan phrases, rejecting causes and negating effects, overreaching their station and going too far—this is like taking rhubarb and croton seeds as one's daily meal. From myself onward, [I shall ensure this does not happen].

The harm caused by such delusions has no end; therefore, as soon as one enters this gate, one treats the Tathāgatas of the ten directions with contempt, claiming for oneself that there is no Buddha to be realized and no practice to be cultivated.
Upon seeing someone recite the Buddha’s name, one says, "The self-nature is itself the Buddha.

Upon seeing someone cultivate the Pure Land, one says, "The mind is itself the Pure Land. Yet, when it comes to discussing Zen meditation, one holds it in the highest esteem, as if it were a celestial realm.

Regarding the aforementioned statement that "reciting the Buddha's name" (nianfo) is superior, it is said to tread upon the nine stages of the earth; whereas "investigating Zen" (can chan) is said to be entirely devoid of thought.
In sum, both are for the sake of resolving birth and death; they are equally bridges for crossing the sea of suffering and precious rafts for transcending the realms.

Since they belong to one and the same family, how can one be superior and the other inferior? Within the gate of investigation, there are also varying depths of realization. As for reciting the Buddha’s name...

The practices cultivated by the multitude also vary in degree; how can you insist that those who participate are of superior capacity while those who merely recite are of middling or inferior capacity? Since the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West and the establishment of this School of the Gate, it has been said that after two hundred years, those who clarify the Way would be many, but those who practice the Way would be few; those who explain the principle would be many, but those who penetrate the principle would be few. As it says in the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp): [Insert relevant excerpt from the Chuan Deng Lu here] ...and so forth. Thus, the masters of the past have already clarified this matter. How can you now, with such arrogance, claim that those who merely recite are not practitioners? This is truly laughable! Furthermore, the Buddha taught that there are four types of people: first, those who hear the Dharma and attain liberation; second, those who see the Dharma and attain liberation; third, those who touch the Dharma and attain liberation; and fourth, those who remember the Dharma and attain liberation. If one does not even reach the level of remembering the Dharma, how can one be called a practitioner? You must realize that the Buddhas and Patriarchs have long since established these categories. Do not harbor such deluded views! If you do not understand this, you will surely fall into the pit of doubt. Be careful! Be careful! Do not let your own mind deceive you. If you wish to avoid being deceived, you must examine yourself thoroughly. Do not merely rely on words and phrases; you must investigate the source of the matter yourself. If you can do this, you will naturally know for yourself whether you are a person of superior, middling, or inferior capacity. Do not be so stubborn as to cling to your own biased views. The hemp and the millet may both be called "grain," yet in reality they are worlds apart. It is the same with those whose affinity for Prajñā is deep and whose spiritual roots were planted in former lives:

whether it be the *gaṅgā* elephant breaking its shell or the fragrant elephant crossing the stream, some perceive the fundamental source in a single phrase, while others manifest majestic power in a single shout.
Upon hearing this once, they awaken a thousand times, attaining the Great Dhāraṇī; or there are those who harbor the aspiration for transcendence and possess the full measure of...
As for your resolve, you must cast aside worldly attachments and investigate this Great Matter; do not rely on minor understandings, but seek only true knowledge.
Lie upon wooden chips, taste gall, drink ice, and swallow bitter gall—practice in this manner for thirty or forty years.

Afterward, if you encounter a wise teacher who pierces you with the needle of painful instruction, your stolen mind will die out and the flower of the mind will finally bloom. Thereafter, you must continue to practice in secret and cultivate in obscurity.
If one eliminates even residual habits and abandons views regarding the Dharma, how much more so should one abandon what is not the Dharma?
If Zhaozhou had excluded even rice porridge and meals, he would have been distracted; if Yongquan, after forty years, still had traces of mental wandering;

or if Xianglin, after forty years, had not achieved a state of being "one piece," remaining ever-vigilant and diligent as if protecting his own head or eyes—only then, when the smoke has vanished and the ashes are extinguished, will a single thought naturally fail to arise.
Karma cannot bind one at the threshold of birth and death; one possesses sovereign mastery according to one's will.

If one examines what has been realized, it seems there may yet be nothing that surpasses the "Highest of the High" rebirth. How is this known? The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna was the patriarch of the fundamental school;
having attained great wisdom and possessing great eloquence, he upheld the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, for several hundred years after the World-Honored One passed away...

Previously, at the assembly on Mount Laṅkā, he bestowed a prediction upon them from afar, yet it did not go beyond saying that they would realize the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
However, according to the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, those of the highest of the high grades are reborn there and, in a single kṣaṇa, also realize the first stage.
Now, even if the great ancestral masters of the Chan school were to see through and transcend all veils and entanglements...

How could words emerging from a mere cliché immediately surpass Nāgārjuna? Since Nāgārjuna has already realized the meaning of non-arising and signlessness and possesses a view that does not fall into hierarchical gradations, his realization is equal to the fruit attained in the "Highest of the High Grades" of rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*).
If this is so, how could the realizations of those in the various Chan schools alone surpass it? This is because the "Highest of the High Grades" [is the pinnacle].

The realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is identical to the awakening of the Chan school; the profound faith in cause and effect is identical to the cultivation of *śamatha* in the Chan school.
The only difference lies in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land.

However, I believe that practitioners of the Chan school who have attained awakening and cultivation neither take up *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* to become equal to the Tathāgata, nor are they willing to take up *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

If one among those of the two vehicles must enter the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices and vows, yet does not cast off one body to receive another in order to deliver sentient beings, then they shall proceed from one land to another to make offerings to all Buddhas;

having seen these Buddhas, they will likewise attain rebirth in the ultimate sense, which—compared to the highest grade of the highest rebirth—is merely a matter of being peers or brothers. Why is this so?
Looking down on the Patriarchs with haughty eyes and speaking lightly of one's pure companions, some may have entered the gate of awakening too early in their rest;
yet if wisdom does not penetrate the subtle, it is difficult to overcome habitual tendencies. As long as a single thought is not exhausted, it remains the root of birth and death.
Driven by the winds of karma, one enters a womb again—just as the Fifth Patriarch’s disciple Jie was reborn as Su Dongpo, and Qing Caotang was reborn as Li Bo (Lugong). The cycle continues.
Following the end of the *yīn* (the five aggregates), one wanders through the realms according to conditions; there is decline but no growth, and karma increases without ever diminishing.
Even if the conditions for *prajñā* are profound enough to avoid falling into the three miserable realms, moving from room to room remains exceedingly arduous.

When one looks back at the multitudes of those born among the middle and lower classes, their misfortune and prosperity are beyond comparison even with heaven and earth—how much more so regarding the spiritual traditions of future generations!
As days pass, people's faculties and capacities likewise decline daily. Although many may give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, it is often insincere and their practice lacks consistency.

Occasionally, one might gain a glimpse of the state of original Buddhahood—the "sudden realization" where the mind-consciousness cannot reach and language cannot express—through the sharp spiritual cues of the Buddhas and Patriarchs or the words of realized masters. Yet, this state is ultimately beyond all conceptualization.
Attainment is itself unattainable, and even the state of non-attainment is unattainable. When one correlates this with the words of the ancients, they do not fail to coincide.
Having attained this understanding of such correspondence, one says: "My seeking has already ceased; I am a man of no affairs.
One recognizes that afflictions are like illusions and thus indulges the emotions to run wild with them; one recognizes that cultivation is fundamentally empty and thus—
To arbitrarily destroy one's practice by claiming that giving (*dāna*) is fundamentally empty, and thus to abandon giving and embrace stinginess;

to claim that patience (*kṣānti*) is fundamentally empty, and thus to listen passively and set aside patience; to speak of precepts (*śīla*) by saying they are fundamentally without observance or violation, asking why one must value strict observance over minor lapses;

and to speak of meditation (*dhyāna*) by saying it is fundamentally without concentration or distraction, asking why one must abandon distraction to attain concentration—such acts follow one’s own emotions and accord with one’s own whims.
When it is said that "treading upon existence is like discoursing on emptiness," and since even dharmas should be relinquished, why would one further grasp at non-dharmas?

Since it is said that even the "True" is not sought, why abandon it to seek after the delusory? Since it is said that the cultivation of contemplation and the practice of meditative concentration all belong to the traces of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), why alone do you crave fame and seek profit, claiming to be in accord with the Way of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? As soon as the fires of love, hatred, defamation, and praise touch you—
When the winds of birth, old age, sickness, and death blow gently upon it, it immediately begins to move; it strives for others and strives for oneself,
asserting "this is right" and "that is wrong," even to the point of taking the nature of fire as one's spirit,
taking pride as one's responsibility, taking guile and deception as one's skillful means, taking deceitful speech as one's expedient, taking license as one's play, and taking foul language as...
They praise those who are lax in discipline and devoid of practice while mocking those who observe every step with meticulous care;

they exclusively manifest the path of principle, thereby exhausting the profound and reaching the ultimate mystery until no trace remains, and by utterly eradicating the gates of practice, they allow the mind to run wild and follow its own whims, casting aside all rules and regulations,
and even claim that oral recitation for rebirth is a teaching of the Lesser Vehicle intended only for preliminary cultivation, after which one may remain in tranquil indifference.
Or, for years on end they do not prostrate before a single Buddha, for years they do not perform a single repentance rite, and for years they do not recite a single sutra;
instead, they look at worldly books that ought not to be read and engage in matters that those who practice the Way should not pursue.

They cause the younger generation to indulge solely in their cleverness, seeking only intellectual understanding; as soon as they acquire some knowledge, they claim to have "leaped directly into" enlightenment.

Furthermore, what more can be said of this frivolous, arrogant, and haughty person who acts with unrestrained license? His mouth utters no words that are not indiscriminate, and his body performs no deeds that are not indiscriminate.
Having already avenged his father, the son proceeds to commit robbery; he transcribes the character for "crow" as "horse," falling into error after error.

He does not consider that worldly passions and desires are boundless—even when dammed, they still overflow. How can one, day after day, use such slick and smooth words to utterly destroy the law of cause and effect?

If one breaks through the gates of these [afflictions], dismantles their barriers and fences, and guides them toward inevitable flow, yet still errs oneself and leads others astray, how can one avoid falling into ruin?
If one is not seized by demons, one will certainly sink forever into the three miserable realms, where the mountains of knives and trees of swords shall requite one's prior causes;
one must shed fur and wear horns to repay past debts. Do not say, "I am a person of realized attainment; karma cannot bind me. This is what is meant.
Karma cannot bind that which is not bound; this does not mean it exists yet is non-existent, but rather that because it is non-existent, it is naturally non-existent from the start.
Since birth follows conditions, how can death not follow karma in receiving rebirth? A single thought of anger in the present moment is itself the form of a monstrous python;
a single thought of greed in the present moment is itself the seed of a hungry ghost. The cause, though formless, is rooted in thought.

Even a minor karmic fruit of form may be exceedingly vast; the subtle consciousness of a single thought-moment sustains it within the field of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), so that even after passing through thousands of millions of kalpas, it is never lost.
For example, because of his wisdom, a certain bhikṣu possessed radiance from his body, yet because of his false speech, maggots flowed from his mouth.
Though the offense was but a single word, such an evil retribution was obtained; despite his wisdom, he could ultimately not eliminate it.
How much more so now, when ignorance and afflictions burn fiercely and are not severed;
to hope to eliminate these evil karmas through a mere semblance of insight and thereby escape the three miserable realms is impossible.

Had these people been content with even a small measure of attainment and had they constantly practiced as taught, never claiming for themselves "I have realized that the mind is Buddha," how could they ever be compared to such [false teachers]?
Those of middle and lower capacities who seek birth through mindfulness of the Buddha must realize that birth is fundamentally non-arising; yet, this does not preclude their fervent seeking of birth.
That very mind is the land, and the Lotus Realm does not exist outside the mind. Do not abandon prostration, do not forsake recitation;

when the power of wisdom and the power of practice advance together like the two wheels of a chariot, one shall then occupy a lotus pedestal of the highest grade and sit within a jeweled pavilion in mid-air for the morning meal.

Fragrant Accumulation has long roamed [the realms], yet when he returned to Pūrṇacandra, he beheld those of the womb-born class shuffling upon jeweled grounds; they heard no words of Dharma and saw no Dharmakāya.

Like elephants and horses that find it difficult to join a herd, or like chickens and phoenixes that are of different species—how much more so for those of the human and celestial realms who dwell in the small fruits of the Path, like mosquitoes and gnats inside a jar!
Thus, with empty bellies and haughty hearts, they cling to emptiness and destroy existence, ultimately succumbing to the delusions of biased attachment.
To understand that one has incurred the fruit of extraordinary retribution—whereby one does not become a child of Amitābha but instead becomes a cause for Yama;
where one does not join the ranks of the pure assembly but instead becomes a companion to the *āpāṅgas*;

where one abandons the Jewel Grove to walk among the sword-trees, and forsakes the Brahma-voice to hear cries of woe—one finds that even the sufferings thus endured cannot yet be compared to those of the ignorant and sightless beings of the world.
If those who perform even minor good deeds and cultivate slight merit are reborn among humans or devas, how vast is the gap between them and those who differ by even a hair’s breadth;

is it not a matter for lamentation? Thus, among those in the Gate of the Patriarchs (the Chan school), those at the highest level may not necessarily transcend to the "Highest Grade of the Highest Birth," while those at the lower levels have already fallen into the three miserable realms. Therefore, one knows that this path is perilous and difficult, not easily traversed.
Success in practice makes one a Buddha; failure makes one a captive of the Mara King. The distinction between these lies in a mere snap of the fingers;

the difference between being cooked [in hell] and liberation is but a hair’s breadth. You ought to choose early between suffering and joy! Furthermore, in this age, the single thread of the gateway to enlightenment is as thin as a strand of silk;
within the Chan school, it is desolate and devoid of people, with only two or three lay practitioners remaining on the direct path.
It is possible to circulate this Dharma; however, since you are a layperson and not a śramaṇa or śākyaputra, you are still bound by the precepts that constrain the body.

To place yourself within the great fire of worldly existence while immersing your mind in the sea of afflictions—though you may have managed to gain a faint entrance into the path amidst your management of worldly affairs—your power of the Way is extremely shallow while the power of karma is extremely deep. Thus, it reaches its limit.
Even coarse karmic actions such as those of lust and killing cannot break the body if one does not practice them; how much less so their subtler forms?

Within the cycle of birth and death, how can one truly escape? We merely observe that those who were ostentatious and extravagant like Yu Di, treacherous and evil like Lü Huíqīng and Xià Sǒng, hasty in their advancement like Zhāng Tiānjué, or refined and licentious like Bái Lètiān and Sū Zǐzhān—all of them [met their end].

To list [this] in the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) and claim that all things are unimpeded is not to understand that although the masters of old possessed right view, if one were to say that they would no longer undergo the retribution of segmented birth (*bhavāṅga-karma*) and could not be bound by it, I dare not grant such a claim.

This is because they were still destined to receive retribution throughout the long night of saṃsāra with no foreseeable end. Therefore, we know that the single gate of Buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*) is especially urgent for a layperson.
Although the power of karma is heavy, by relying upon the Buddha’s power one may avoid sinking into the depths;
like a debtor hidden within the royal palace who cannot be held liable for repayment, once born into the Buddha-land, all that one has realized and understood throughout life will not be in vain.
Death hastens us on while our breath is difficult to preserve; seek the path home early to avoid being caught in the turmoil, even if your resolve is set upon Chan meditation.
It is not at all a hindrance to practice *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation) alongside one's worldly duties as an official or a householder;

it is said that even these do not obstruct the path, let alone the morning and evening prostrations and recitations. Furthermore, by borrowing the urgency of *nienfo*, one can awaken the mind for *chan* (meditative inquiry);
by borrowing the profound penetration of the gate of *chan*, one can solidify the faith in the Pure Land. These two aspects support one another, making the practice most stable.
Truly, those who do not believe this are exactly like the most ignorant. Layman Shitou has long aspired to investigate Chan;
his spiritual capacity is sharp and keen, and within ten years he attained profound penetration. His mental acuity is swift and sharp, and his speech is perfectly fluid and turning.

Whenever he discusses this matter with others, he can produce a thousand words upon taking up the pen; he does not tread upon the phrases of the Patriarchs, but flows directly from the depths of his own breast.
Producing living tigers and living dragons, there was not a single word that failed to convey life; he thus also claimed for himself realization and felt there was nothing more to do.

Although his worldly attachments diminished and he did not enter the dust and toil of the mundane world, he still indulged in mocking the wind and playing with the moon, climbing mountains and gazing at flowing waters, frequenting circles of literature and wine, and immersing himself in the refined pursuits of poetry and elegance. Yet, being indolent, arrogant, and reckless, he could not help but indulge his impulses as before.
I have not yet been able to fully escape this illness; fortunately, my sense of urgency regarding birth and death is keen, so that I do not remain long submerged in it.
I feel deep pain thinking of how the mind arises upon encountering objects and how every path one touches becomes a hindrance. Superficial understanding cannot truly overcome actual reality;

if awakening is not followed by cultivation, one will inevitably fall into demonic realms. The distinction between Buddha and Mara lies in a mere moment. Thus, I have begun to restrain my biased view of emptiness and enter into the realm of Samantabhadra.

Furthermore, when reflecting upon the definitive essence of the gateways of practice, I found none more excellent than the recitation of the Buddha’s name; yet, as for those of middling and inferior capacities who were led by provisional means, their doubts had not been entirely dispelled.

Later, through extensive study of the sūtras and śāstras, I first realized that this gateway fundamentally subsumes the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), and that it is appropriate for both those who have attained awakening and those who have not to cultivate it.
Thereupon, I gathered what was proclaimed by the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha] and elucidated by the Bodhisattvas.

The various great spiritual friends have brought forth these teachings, which, though augmented by their own personal insights— arising like a thousand waves and flowing like ten thousand diverging streams—
when traced back to their ultimate convergence, all stem from a single source. This treatise takes the inconceivable ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as its core principle, uses awakening as its guide,
and maintains the recitation of the Buddha’s name throughout the twelve periods of the day with a single mind, free from distraction, such that every thought-moment is continuous.
I shall continue to practice by taking the ten thousand practices of the six perfections as auxiliary causes and deep faith in cause and effect as the gateway.

As soon as this treatise was completed, five fellow practitioners who had resolved their minds, upheld the precepts, and recited the Buddha’s name, desired to circulate it together in order to resolve the delusions regarding doctrine and practice.
Xiangguang has dull faculties and weak discernment; for a long time, he has been intoxicated by the view of emptiness.
Indulging his passions and following his whims like a mad elephant, he once last year, during a night of deep intoxication, personally visited the Gridhaka Hell.
There, amidst blazing fires, he saw the emaciated and lame forms of monks whom he had previously known to preach emptiness yet had violated their precepts as they passed by;
the sound of their wailing shook the earth, nearly unbearable to hear. Upon waking, the hair on his body stood on end, and he immediately resolved to return to the path.
"Having relied upon the *Pure Land Sūtras*, you now read this treatise; thus, long-standing doubts are dissolved like ice. Therefore, today do not shrink from bitter words:
a sick man knows a physician, and a profligate pities a guest. You should utterly eradicate your former views and study with an empty mind;
entry [into the Way] will surely come of itself. The matter of birth and death is great—do not hesitate for long. Thereupon, the Chan practitioner’s tears welled up in sorrow.
He said, "Had I not met you, my son, I would have spent my entire life deceived by the view of emptiness. You have truly brought me back to life.
He earnestly requested that [the Master] compile his collected works, prostrated himself, and departed. This was on the twenty-third day of the second month of the Gengzi year of the Wanli era.

Now, to cling to forms and delude the mind is the fault of conditioned existence; to dwell on emptiness and destroy existence leads to the calamity of chaos. For this reason, Bodhidharma...
To save those who cling to signs, he taught that both sin and merit are entirely empty.

During the Yongming era, he spoke to refute the followers of wild wisdom, saying that while the totality of the ten thousand virtues is like water for extinguishing fire, once the water has passed, there is the calamity of drowning;

and while that which gives life flourishes day by day, it becomes the very basis for withering and scorching. The Tathāgata’s teaching is also like this, as the Five Leaves [of the Huayan school] have shown.
The tradition of single-lineage transmission flourished until it reached the present day, where its excesses have become extreme;
erroneous interpretations equate "mind-only" with the non-Buddhist path of non-action, and such dogmatic assertions lead one toward the demonic city of the five desires.

One fails to reflect that Ānanda had not yet attained full mastery and was consequently expelled for his ascetic practices, or that Mātaṅga was rebuked by the Venerable One for his slight attachment to fetters, or that Śāriputra was disparaged for his meager cultivation of the jewel-like precepts.

Regarding these distant hills and mountains, amidst the clusters of defilement and purity, from where could joy possibly arise? If the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was transmitted by Bodhidharma, then both awakening and cultivation were equally valued;

yet the pure regulations were first established at Baizhang, where vehicle and precepts were practiced together. Never before had the fundamental principles of the One Vehicle been heard, nor had the Pure Precepts been so reviled.
The legitimate heirs of the Five Lamps were greedily attached to worldly conditions. Formerly, there was a Daoist who, while walking at night, was encountered by a ghost.
While he was lying dazed among the graves, an old farmer saw him and helped him into his house; only after being bathed with hot water did he regain consciousness.
As the Daoist was about to depart, he said to the farmer, "I am a traveler and have nothing to give you as a gift, but I have two talismans for warding off ghosts;
I offer them as my thanks. Those who heard this laughed at him. Yet, the scholars of today burn with greed, anger, and false views like a raging fire.
To wish to untie the bonds of others while being so deluded oneself—how strange! I studied the Way for ten years before falling into this madness.
Later, upon encountering a catalyst, I attained a slight awakening; I then simplified my worldly affairs and turned my heart toward the Pure Land.

In the intervals between my prostrations, recitations, and chanting, I took up the treatises of Nāgārjuna, Tiantai, Fazhao, and Yongming, reading them with meticulous care. Suddenly, my doubts were cleared away, and I gained deep conviction.
In the Pure Land, I further awakened to the diverse practices of the great Bodhisattvas, like a poor child who has discovered gold in a hidden treasure and cannot contain his joy.
When Master Yuyan and Layman Pingqian planned for me to compile various treatises on the Western Paradise,
I then recorded the essential words of the ancient masters and appended my own views, binding them into a single volume titled *Xi* (The West).
This treatise was begun on the twenty-third day of the tenth month of the Jihai year and completed on the twenty-second day of the twelfth month.
As it has been subject to limited revision, there are many omissions; however, wishing to provide a skillful means for beginners, I hope that those of the Way will correct it.

1. The Gate of the Buddha-lands; 2. The Gate of Dependent Origination; 3. The Gate of Scriptural Categories; 4.
The Gate of the Characteristics of the Teachings; 5. The Gate of Principles and Truths; 6. The Gate of Accordance with Nature;
7. The Gate of Rebirth; 8. The Gate of the Net of Views; 9. The Gate of Cultivation and Maintenance.

First, the Gate of Buddha-lands:
Within the single true Dharma-realm, body and land interpenetrate; throughout the oceans of ten Buddha-lands, there is no distinction between the pure and the defiled.
It is solely because the karmic actions of sentient beings differ that the manifestations of the Buddhas also vary—whether provisional or real, partial or perfect, or otherwise.

Whether temporary or permanent, gradual or sudden, a single moon is fully contained within the ripples of a thousand rivers for a month, and a single lamp in a room manifests its full radiance in every light.
This principle—that the One Truth is inherently one yet its manifestations differ in a thousand ways—is not something sentient beings can grasp without the extensive citation of sacred texts.
Therefore, I shall briefly outline ten gates based on the various teachings.
1. The Pure Land of Vairocana; 2. The Pure Land of Mind-Only; 3.
The Pure Land of Constant Reality; 4. The Pure Land of Manifestation; 5. The Pure Land of Rebirth; 6. The Pure Land of Emanated Bodies;
7. The Pure Land of Dependence; 8. The Pure Lands of All Directions.
9. The inconceivable pure land of the fourfold purification through single-mindedness;
10. The inconceivable pure land that gathers in and sustains all sentient beings of the ten directions.
Regarding the first, the Pure Land of Vairocana: this is the fundamental retributive land of all Buddhas. 10. The Lotus Treasury World...
In each of the lotus-matrix worlds within the ocean of realms, at the very bottom, there are vast lands as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds, all pure and magnificently adorned.

Each of these vast lands is further surrounded by minor lands as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds, increasing in size and extent in successive multiples. Thus, every Flower-Matrix World completely fills space.
They penetrate one another, encompassing both the pure and the defiled in infinite layers;

according to the Dharma, every blade of grass, every tree, every hair, and every speck of dust each and all possesses this inexhaustible Dharma-realm. Buddhas and sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction.
Someone might say: "This [Flower Treasury World] is the actual reward-adornment of sentient beings, which differs from the provisional teachings that project the Pure Land elsewhere."

This alone constitutes the True Teaching. Some may say: "Though sentient beings possess this true retribution, how can they realize it for themselves, given that True Suchness (Tathatā) lacks inherent nature?
In this vast and long night, there is no date for seeing the light; in these surging waves of kalpas, there is no time for reaching the shore.

Yet, though it is said that the mind of wondrous enlightenment arises within hell and the fruit of Buddhahood manifests within the realm of the hells (niraya), what can be done about the reality before one's very eyes?"
Why are there iron beds and copper pillars? They are used to ward off hungry ghosts who die of thirst by the seashore, or for the poor man who counts coins in a golden cave;

he sees only their emptiness—how can they be called real? If it were not for these provisional skillful means, by which one enters the real through expedient power, how could sentient beings ever have the day of realizing Vairocana?
He replied: "If we speak in terms of the transformative rituals of the Buddhas, then it is so."
Within the realm of true reality (*dharmatā*), such conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) does not exist.
Indeed, Vairocana—translated here as "Pervading All Places"—is synonymous with Amitāyus; how could there be any distinction of superiority or inferiority?
It is solely for the sake of those ordinary beings who grasp at signs that the Tathāgata speaks of Amitābha being in the Western Quarter, just as it is stated in the *Mahāmegha Sūtra*.
Amitābha Buddha addressed a bodhisattva, saying: "There is Śākyamuni in the Sahā world.
When Śākyamuni is taken as the subject, then Śākyamuni pervades all things, and Amitābha is but one location among those pervaded.
When Amitābha is taken as the subject, then Amitābha pervades all things, and Śākyamuni is but one location among those pervaded."
In one place, as in the body of a single person: when it is the "self" of that self, it does not hinder its being the "other" of all other persons;
and when it is the "other" of those others, it does not hinder its being the "self" of all other persons. For this reason, self and other are not established as fixed entities.
Since self and other are not established, the self likewise pervades all places, and the other likewise pervades all places; how could they possibly exist as determinate [entities]?
Therefore, others may hold that the Vairocana of the Western Quarter is not [the universal] self-and-other. Why is this? Because Vairocana is all-pervading.

If one speaks of him as provisional or as a skillful means (*upāya*), then there would be that which is not all-pervading; and if there were that which is not all-pervading, the meaning of Vairocana would not be established.
Second, regarding the Pure Land of Mind-Only: it is to directly realize for oneself that the very essence of non-mind is itself the Pure Land.
As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Ratnakūṭa, you should know that the straightforward mind is the bodhisattva’s pure land;

when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who are not sycophantic will come to be born in that land. The profound mind is the bodhisattva’s pure land; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood..."
Sentient beings who possess sufficient merit and have the mind of the Mahāyāna come to be born in that land; this is the pure land of a bodhisattva.

When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings of the Mahāyāna come to be born in that land. The scriptural passages are numerous and cannot be cited in full, but the general meaning is that if one wishes to obtain a pure land, one must purify one's own mind.
According to the purity of one's mind, so too is the Buddha-land purified. Now, as for the mind...
The land is precisely the mind; the land is the mind. That the mind is pure and the land is pure is the natural law (*dharmatā*).

Is this statement not a commentary on the Western Paradise? Many who cling to the mind disparage this Dharma gate, considering it a teaching for those of dull faculties alone, because they perceive the land as existing outside the mind.
Indeed, mindfulness is itself the mind; is the recitation of the Buddha's name not precisely this?

The mind is pure; the mind fundamentally contains the land of the lotus paradise, for how could it exist outside the mind? Thus we know that while [the teachings] concerning phenomenal appearances do not contradict the principle of "mind-only," they accord with the reality of the mind so as to universally deliver all beings.
Third, regarding the eternally true pure land: this refers to the pure land indicated during the assembly on Vulture Peak, which was taught as a provisional means within the Three Vehicles.

The teaching instructs bodhisattvas to know that this land is inherently pure despite its appearance of defilement; yet while the multitudes believe this, they do not yet see it. For the nature of defilement is fundamentally quiescent and conventional appearances are eternally empty.

Because it is fundamentally quiescent, the bodhisattva dwells in defilement while remaining ever-quiescent; because conventional appearances are eternally empty, the bodhisattva enters the mundane world while remaining eternally empty.

This precisely manifests the meaning of purity. However, because the ocean of sentient beings' attachments is difficult to clear and the rope of their consciousness is easy to bind, [this truth remains hidden].

To say that karma is fundamentally empty and thus act with unrestrained license, or to claim that words and deeds have no substance and thus proceed in darkness as one pleases—this leads to the reproaches of Yongjia and the fall of Shanxing.
Those who reach the point where they encounter royal peril in life or become the retinue of Māra in death are indeed numerous.
Alas! If the entire earth were filled with Bodhisattvas, then these words would truly be beneficial.
If Bodhisattvas who benefit the world are few while ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are many, then the benefit to the world from such words will be slight,
whereas the harm to the world will be great.

As for the fourfold manifestation of the Pure Land, it is as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the Pure Land was transformed three times and all humans and devas were moved and placed therein.
Furthermore, in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, the World-Honored One pressed the earth with his toe,
and immediately this trichiliocosm was adorned with hundreds of thousands of rare jewels; this was a temporary manifestation by the Tathāgata,

yet it is also the natural law (*dharmatā*) that even one as wise as Śāriputra is like a blind man, and sentient beings of inferior faculties have no opportunity to see it again— let alone humans and devas.
In all other directions, there is entirely no karmic affinity for guidance; though spiritual powers may manifest briefly, they vanish again. How could these be permanent lands?

How can they compare to the Pure Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), which endures through kalpas as many as motes of dust, where the Compassionate Father Amitābha does not reject even those who have committed the ten evils?
The superiority and inferiority of these lands are clearly evident.
Fifth, regarding the Pure Land of Retribution for Others: it is like the realm of Maheśvara (i.e., Akaniṣṭha Heaven). It is there that the Tathāgata attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment;

this is the Pure Land of True Retribution. The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states: "When the Bodhisattva’s merits are fully perfected, he manifests a body that is the highest and greatest in all worlds within the realm of Akaniṣṭha;
that is to say, by means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, ignorance is suddenly [extinguished]."
All that is called the "unconceivable activity of the self-existent Sarvākārajñatā (all-aspect wisdom)" is able to manifest throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings.
Master Zang asked: "For what reason does the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) reside in this heaven? [The answer is:

It is because it relies upon the ten kings of the hells to manifest the distinctions of the ten stages (bhūmis). [In each stage, the manifested body is different. The tenth stage is entrusted to this Heavenly King; thus, within that very body (referring to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, which refers to the tenth stage), he manifests the attainment of Bodhi.

However, although those devas are said to be without outflows (*anāsrava*), they do not compare to the Lotus Land, which directly transcends the three realms. Why is this? Because it resides at the very summit of the realm of form (*akaniṣṭha*).
Regarding the pure lands of the six-part body, as the Buddha replied to King Kalyāṇakāma in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Good son..."

To the west of this Sahā world, passing through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of thirty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Anabhibhūta, which is like the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī). I appeared in that land for the sake of transforming sentient beings;
thus, I manifest here in this world to turn the wheel of Dharma. Furthermore, in the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*, the Buddha said to Aṅgulimāla:
Mañjuśrī said, "I abide in the limit of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmatā*), yet you do not perceive it.
Ugra asked, "If you abide in the limit of non-arising, why are you born in this land? The Buddha said, "There is a Buddha in the eastern direction; go and ask him.
Mañjuśrī went and questioned that Buddha, who replied, "Śākyamuni is none other than my own body. The general meaning is that that Pure Land is the Buddha’s true reality.

The response states that although this is the retribution of a manifested body (nirmāṇakāya) of a single Buddha, its realm of retribution does not yet fully encompass the meaning of gathering and transforming beings;
for while it exists from the perspective of the Buddha's own division, it is absent from the perspective of sentient beings' division, and thus it is not particularly sublime.
Regarding the seven types of dependent pure lands, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "I, Vairocana, now sit upon the lotus pedestal;
surrounding me on a thousand petals are a thousand Śākyamunis. On each petal are ten billion lands, and in each land is one Śākyamuni.
This means that because those at the first bhūmi transform a hundred buddha-fields, there are flowers with a hundred petals; those at the second bhūmi transform a thousand.

In the Buddha-fields, the original lotuses have one thousand petals; upon reaching the third stage (*bhūmi*), one should see ten thousand petals, and at the fourth stage, a hundred million petals, increasing sequentially by multiples of ten.
This is because these are manifestations of the *paratantra-paribhogātmabhāva* (the body for the enjoyment of others) shown as the realm of retribution;
they are seen only after entering the stages, unlike the case in the Lotus Assembly where sentient beings with ten recitations suddenly behold the pure Buddha-land.

Regarding the pure lands of the various directions: for instance, there is the Pure Land of Bhaisajyaguru Buddha in the east, the Pure Land of Candrasūryapradīpa Buddha in the south, and the Pure Land of Gandhottamakūṭa Buddha in the zenith.
As described in various sūtras, these cannot be recorded in full; they are all the adornments of the true retribution (*vipāka*) of the Buddhas.
In some sūtras, these lands are temporarily made manifest through the supernatural power of a Buddha, or by great bodhisattvas...
When the Bodhisattva went there to make offerings, because that Buddha had not yet spoken of gathering in sentient beings, those beings likewise had no cause to be born there.

That world is like the world of Sukhāvatī; although Śākyamuni has recorded that there are those who will be reborn there, I have not yet heard any statement from Akṣobhya regarding a universal invitation [of all beings].
Furthermore, that land contains Mount Cakravāḍa, Mount Sumeru, and various mountains, as well as malevolent spirits and women.
One should know that the adornment and purification [of other lands] does not equal that of An-yang (Sukhāvatī).
Furthermore, in the *Sūtra on the Twelve Great Vows of Bhaisajyaguru Tathāgata for Delivering All Sentient Beings*, it is also said: "Those who possess faith should be reborn there.

While one may rely upon those vows, they mostly result in liberation from all sorrow and suffering and ultimate peace and happiness; yet this is not comparable to the fact that Amitābha Tathāgata purely employs [these means].
Reciting the Buddha's name encompasses all people for rebirth in that land.
Regarding the nine aspects of single-mindedness and the four kinds of Pure Lands: first is the Land of Common Dwelling of Ordinary Beings and Sages;

second is the Land of Traceless Skillful Means; third is the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction; and fourth is the Land of Eternal Quiescence and Radiance. First, the Land of Common Dwelling of Ordinary Beings and Sages...
Regarding the lands where beings dwell, there are two categories: first, the impure land of cohabitation; second, the pure land of cohabitation.

Within the impure land, there are two types of dwellings for ordinary beings and two for noble ones. The two dwellings for ordinary beings are: first, evil sentient beings, which refers to the four realms of existence;

and second, virtuous sentient beings, which refers to humans and devas. The two dwellings for noble ones are: first, actual noble ones, which includes those of the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] and pratyekabuddhas; and second, [provisional noble ones].

The teachings for the six stages—the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) and the ten faiths (*daśaśraddhā*)—are distinct; although delusions are exhausted at the final stage of the ten faiths, the retribution body (*vipākakāya*) still remains, and these are all termed "real.

The two types of provisional sages refer to the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas within the lands of Expedient Means, True Reward, and Peaceful Light, as well as the Buddhas of Wondrous Enlightenment who manifest in the Land of Common Dwelling out of compassion for those with karmic affinity—all of these are "provisional. These [beings] and those in the four miserable realms...

Because they dwell together, it is called a defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra*). Next, regarding those who dwell together in a pure land: as in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), there are sentient beings;
or as in the Land of Supreme Joy (*Abhirati*), there are the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) and men and women. Because the four evil destinies (*apāya*) are absent, it is called a pure land.

According to my own analysis, within the defiled lands where we dwell together, since various sages are already present, these may also be termed "pure lands of cohabitation," such as [the case of] Saha.

The Sahā world is located within the thirteenth layer of the Flower Store World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu), which is also called the Flower Store. Second, regarding the Land of Residual Skillful Means (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*):

for those of the Two Vehicles and the three types of Bodhisattvas who have destroyed the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*) and realized the Path of Skillful Means, yet have not yet severed the "dust-sand" specific delusions and ignorance (*avidyā*), they cast off their bodies of segmented existence (*paricchinna-deha*) and are born outside the realm; therefore, it is called "Residual. Thus it is explained.
The treatise states: "Outside the triple world there is a Pure Land where Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born;

they receive a Dharma-nature body, not a body of segmented birth. Third, the Land of Real Reward and Non-obstruction is the dwelling place of those free from the two vehicles, consisting purely of Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body.
Having exhausted dust-like delusions and partially shattered ignorance, they attain the fruit of reality. And so forth.

Because it is the Dharma-nature Reward Body that receives the fruition of untainted karma when the illumination has not yet reached its ultimate limit, it is also called the Land of Fruitional Reward. Thus, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states:

"The Three Worthies and Ten Sages dwell in the Land of Fruitional Reward; by contemplating the true aspect [of reality], they give rise to genuine untaintedness, and their resulting retribution is so sublime as to be adorned with the seven treasures and endowed with the pure and wondrous five sensory objects;
therefore, it is called the 'True' [Land]. Here, matter and mind are non-dual, and every hair-pore contains a world-system."

Because they are mutually compatible, they are called "unobstructed"; this refers to the world of Indra’s Net as clarified in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Fourth, regarding the Land of Constant Quiescent Light:
the Suchness-Dharmadhātu illuminated by the ultimate wisdom of wondrous enlightenment is termed a "land" (*kṣetra*) and is also called the "Dharma-nature Land.
However, while the single True Suchness Buddha-nature is neither body nor land, it is spoken of in terms of body and land; yet apart from the body, there is no [land].
When earth is separated from earth, there is no body; this is the dwelling place where all Buddhas and Tathāgatas roam and reside. The *Miaozong* (Essential Commentary) states:

"What the sūtras and śāstras refer to as the 'tranquil light' (*śāntaprabhā*) being 'without marks' (*animitta*) means that the marks of defilement and obstruction have been completely exhausted; it is not like the great void of space where nothing exists at all.

This is because when the three delusions are ultimately purified, the colors and mind of both the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) become ultimately manifest. The Great Sūtra says:
By the cessation of these [conditioned] forms, one attains eternal form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

The Benevolent King Sūtra calls this the "five aggregates of dharma-nature" (distinct from the five aggregates of the physical body). This is the ultimate reality. Furthermore, throughout the lands of the ten directions, things are seen differently according to the mind:

what for some is of the seven treasures may for others be sand and gravel, differing according to their respective locations. Thus, Xiachuan said: "The Land of Ultimate Bliss consists of four different types of lands. Why is this? It is because..."
The two vehicles of humans and devas correspond to the former two kinds of lands, while the Bodhisattvas and Buddhas correspond to the latter two kinds of lands.
Therefore, one should know that although there are bodies [measuring] six million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sands of *yojanas*, it does not preclude the existence of bodies sixteen feet tall;
and although there are boundless Buddha-lands within the Flower Treasury Ocean assembly, it does not preclude the existence of the land by the Nairañjanā River. Why is this so?
Therefore, this is due to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and is not a manifestation through supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
Regarding the inconceivable pure land that encompasses all sentient beings of the ten directions:
this refers to the Western Pure Land of Amitābha Buddha, wherein exists an ocean of great merit, an ocean of great compassionate wisdom, and the power of great vows.
If Sea-If were to explain it in full— suppose all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, devas, humans, ghosts, and animals throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
down to the smallest flying insects, wriggling creatures, and all insentient things such as grasses, trees, tiles, pebbles, and atoms of *paramāṇu*—
if each of these were to possess infinite mouths, and within each mouth infinite tongues; and if each tongue...
From within each [of these], immeasurable sounds emerge, constantly speaking, repeatedly speaking, fervently speaking, and speaking without interruption;
even after hundreds of billions of *koṭi* of *rajas* *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they could not be exhausted. Now, I shall briefly explain: first, the inconceivability of the body and the land;
second, the inconceivability of nature and characteristics; third, the inconceivability of cause and effect; and fourth, coming and going.
The Fivefold Meaning of the Inconceivable: First, the meaning of the inconceivability of the body and land:
Within the body of Amitābha, there are immeasurable sentient beings; likewise, within the bodies of sentient beings, there are immeasurable lands of Amitābha.
Therefore, when a single sentient being recollects Amitābha, that Amitābha perceives all those sentient beings.
When one contemplates Amitābha, Amitābha sees sentient beings; when one contemplates Amitābha in every thought-moment, Amitābha sees in every thought-moment.
If there were no Amitābha within the bodies of sentient beings, Amitābha would not see them—just as one cannot obtain water from a sun-crystal if it is not inherently present within it.
Likewise, if there were no sentient beings within the body of Amitābha, Amitābha would also not see them—just as [water is not produced] from a stone.

If a woman seeks to give birth to a son, it cannot be obtained because it is not what ought to be obtained. Therefore, within the body there is contained the body; within the body there is contained the body;

within the body and the land there is contained the land; within the land and the land there is contained the land and the body. Thus, the body and the land contain one another in layers without end; this is the meaning of the inconceivability of the body and the land.
Regarding the meaning of the inconceivability of the mutual characteristics of the two natures: if one were to speak apart from the natures...
Earth and earth are, outside of mind, illusory transformations; that which is an illusory transformation is the characteristic of cessation. Sentient beings do not arise [from it].
If one speaks in terms of essence (*dhātu*), the essence of earth has form, and because it is determinate, that which is determinate is without change.

That which is without change means sentient beings also do not arise. Essence is identical with appearance, yet neither appearance nor non-appearance exists; they are not non-existent, nor are they lost.

The meaning that existence is itself destruction is the principle of the inconceivability of nature and characteristics. Third, regarding the meaning of the inconceivability of cause and effect, there are two aspects:
first, the principle of the cause preceding and the effect following—namely, mindfulness of the Buddha is the cause and seeing the Buddha is the effect;

seeing the Buddha is the cause and attaining Buddhahood is the effect; attaining Buddhahood is the cause and saving sentient beings is the effect. Second, the principle of cause and effect being without before or after.
Meaning is itself mindfulness, itself vision, itself accomplishment, and itself deliverance; it is fully present all at once. It is like a person who is thirty and then reaches forty:
thirty is the cause and forty is the result. Between thirty and forty there is no interval. If there were no thirty, forty would not be established;
if there were no thirty, forty could not be accomplished. Therefore, one should know that they are not separate from one another.
From thirty to forty: if one were to depart from the state between thirty and forty, there would be a mark of limitation in the interval;
yet this body of mine has no such limitation. If it were by way of proceeding from thirty to forty, there would be a mark of continuity in the interval;
yet in this body of mine, even continuity cannot be found. Thus one contemplates the cause and effect of mindfulness of the Buddha.
It is also like this; this is the meaning of the inconceivability of cause and effect. Fourth, regarding the meaning of the inconceivability of coming and going:
if Amitābha Buddha comes here because of mindfulness, and these sentient beings are born there because of recollecting the Buddha, then there would be coming and going.
Where there is coming and going, there is a path; where there is a path, there are difficulties and ease, just as for one who approaches the capital.

Thus, an audience with the Lord is easy when near, but difficult when far. If this were truly the case regarding the mindfulness of the Buddha and the seeking of birth [in his land], there would have to be ease and difficulty;
furthermore, Amitābha would be constantly traveling on the road and would have no day to preach the Dharma. Therefore, the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* says:
"One does not end one's life here to be born in that other Buddha-field; the Buddha comes from nowhere, and I likewise go nowhere. Furthermore, previously...

The arising of virtue is definitively arising, yet its departing is truly not departing. It is like the sounding of a celestial drum, heard equally from far and near, because it neither comes nor goes.
It is like the moon in water: when one moves eastward, the moon moves east; when one moves westward, the moon moves west, because it neither comes nor goes.
This is the meaning of the inconceivability of coming and going. Fifth, regarding the meaning of the ultimate inconceivability: as it is said...
The mountain’s reflection in the clear pool is like the spring sun; the hundred grasses are like the karmic power of sentient beings; their appearance is like the light of the sun and moon;
the faculties within the womb are like the self within the body; the teeth are firm while the tongue is supple;

the brows are horizontal while the hair is long—this is the ultimate inconceivable meaning of the inconceivable. Thus, even when the Buddhas of the ten directions pour out their hearts and entrails, it is only this.

It can only be said that this is something rare and difficult to believe; even with the mark of a tongue that covers the three thousand great thousandfold worlds, how could one possibly explain even a ten-thousandth part of it?
Confucius said, "The ignorance of a common husband and wife can participate in knowledge, yet when it comes to the ultimate, even a sage does not know.
How profound these words are! They show that the immeasurable Dharma-gates are all unified by a single principle.
