The man thought to himself, "Both ghosts possess great power; if I speak a lie, I will surely die. It is better to tell the truth. He replied, "The first ghost brought it.
The second ghost became furious, seized the man by the hand, tore it off, and threw it to the ground. The first ghost then took an arm from the corpse and attached it [to the man].
Immediately, his two arms, two legs, head, and sides—his entire body—were transformed. Then the two ghosts together devoured the person's transformed flesh, wiped their mouths, and departed.
The man reflected: "I see with my own eyes that my body has been eaten away by the ghosts;
this body of mine is now entirely the flesh of others. Thereupon, at all times, he maintained the perception of it as another's body, even unto death.
One does not crave or cling to the five desires because they belong to another; therefore, one should not make offerings to them.
Even toward one's wife and children, one does not give rise to defilement because they belong to another; therefore, there should be no attachment to them.

Even when subjected to various forms of rebuke and suffering, one accepts them all with compliance because they belong to another, and thus there is no further arrogance. Later, if one were suddenly to calculate that "if this [self] were another," it would not be so.
If the self were not other than the other, then within the present body of another, it would be neither other nor non-other, neither self nor non-self;
thus, neither self nor other could be apprehended. From the very beginning, it has always been thus.
At that moment, one realizes that all phenomena—whether self or non-self—are merely false conceptualizations. This is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
The power of inconceivable contemplation for seeing Buddhas in oneself and others is likewise so.

It is also like the poor man Shang Jiu Kai, who, believing the words of a wealthy man, entered fire without being burned, entered water without drowning, and threw himself from a height without breaking;
even following all the deceiver's words, he obtained real treasures. Yet this poor man had no other skill; it was because of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [who empowered him].
It is likewise with the attainment of the King of Jewels, the Buddha, through inconceivable desire. It is also like an empty valley that echoes in response to a sound:
this echo does not come from the sky, nor does it come from the valley, nor does it come from the sound itself. If it came from the sky, the sky would always have echoes;
if it came from the valley, it would echo at all times; if it came from the sound, then when one calls out, [the echo would arise].
At that time, this resonance is transmitted even to the earth; it does not come from a combination of conditions, nor does it come from causes and conditions, nor does it arise spontaneously.
The mark of the inconceivable sound of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise neither coming nor going.
Furthermore, it is like a phantom person or a phantom horse beloved by a wealthy elder, which enters into a small bottle; the bottle does not increase in size, yet the horse leaps within it.

Just as when the Elder Śroṇa had prepared food, the horse remained tied to its pillar as before, so too is it with the manifestation of Buddha-fields by the inconceivable illusory power of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, it is like the *hañjikā* elixir:
if a person obtains even one *liang* of it, they can transform a thousand *liang* of copper entirely into pure gold; it is not the thousand *liang* of copper that can transform this [elixir].
The inconceivable great elixir of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva that transforms impurity into purity by a single application is also like this.
Furthermore, it is like a person who obtains añjana medicine and applies it to their eyes; though they walk among people, they are not seen by others.
Likewise, through the inconceivable power of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s medicine, in every moment of thought, one attains the body of non-arising (*anutpāda-kāya*).
Furthermore, it is like the "Invincible" fragrance; if it is applied to a drum, when its sound is struck, all enemy armies will spontaneously retreat and disperse.
Again, the Universal Monarch possesses a fragrance called "Ocean Treasury"; if a single pellet is burned, the king and his fourfold army can all soar through the air.
So too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s inconceivable fragrance of right mindfulness subdue all Māras.
The army’s transcendence of the three realms is likewise thus. Therefore, one should know that the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) is inconceivable;

it is as inconceivable as the pores of Samantabhadra, as inconceivable as the womb of Queen Māyā, as inconceivable as the room of one cubit of Vimalakīrti, and as inconceivable as the small vessel of the laywoman Guḍaśaṅkhā.

The discussion asks: For what reason are all phenomena (*dharma*) inconceivable? If there were even a hair’s breadth of anything that could be conceived, it would not be the nature-ocean of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
As stated above, speaking of mind, speaking of objects, or speaking of having marks or being markless—all these are conceivable phenomena.
If one enters this inconceivable liberation, one then knows all conceptual discriminations.
To recite the Buddha’s name is entirely conceptual proliferation.
*The Compendium of the Western Regions*, Scroll Five;
*The Compendium of the Western Regions*, Scroll Six.
The sixth is the gate of conforming to the nature [of reality].
Indeed, all worthies and sages act in accordance with their minds; the dharma-nature is boundless, and the ocean of their conduct is immeasurable.

Therefore, some may fulfill the practices of three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in a single moment, while others may not complete even a single thought for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges. They are like birds flying through the sky.
The traces distinguish the boundaries of the stages; the tears shed like wind-blown flowers clarify the images of the past and present.
Without needing to run, one reaches the presence of Amitābha; why is it not swift?

It is because one realizes that the Western Land is not far away—just as among the five colors, black is the ultimate depth, and among the myriad streams, the ocean is the final destination. Now, summarizing the various practices of the Mahāyāna:
Entering into the single practice is briefly shown through five gates:
first, the practice of faith; second, the practice of calm abiding and insight; third, the practice of the six perfections;
fourth, the practice of compassion and vows; and fifth, the practice of accord with the Dharma.

Regarding the practitioner of single-minded faith, a sutra states: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of all merit; there are no practices whatsoever that do not take faith as their primary cause.
This holds true until the fruit of Bodhi is fully realized; it is simply the perfection of this faculty of faith. It is like a grain of rice falling to the earth:

when it reaches the stage of ripening, it is no different from its original seed. Or like a young bamboo shoot reaching the heavens: from its initial sprout to its eventual dense foliage, the root remains the same.
This is because there are no Bodhisattvas of original aspiration who do not achieve accomplishment by relying upon this power of faith;
therefore, within the Lotus School, one relies entirely upon this faith as the root.

First, one must believe that the Immovable Wisdom and Fundamental Wisdom of Amitābha Buddha are no different from one's own—like the great void of space, which is bright when the sun shines and obscured when clouds come.
Since empty space is fundamentally non-existent, clouds and the sun are both identical to that very space;

therefore, I truly believe that all the various practices of difficult deeds and endurance performed by Amitābha Buddha from the time he first made his vow throughout *nayuta* kalpas, I too am able to perform.
Why? Because I recall myself drifting and drowning in the three [realms] throughout beginningless kalpas.
One can endure the suffering of birth, the suffering of death, the suffering of wearing fur and bearing horns, the suffering of the iron beds and copper pillars, and all manner of useless sufferings;
how much more so, then, the myriad practices for saving sentient beings as performed by Bodhisattvas today—how could one not be able to do this?
Third, one must have faith in Amitābha Buddha’s immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable spiritual powers, and his accomplishments.
"I shall likewise attain such matters as [the Buddha's] measure and power of vows. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s own nature and skillful means possess such inconceivable matters, and I share the same single essence of pure nature as the Tathāgata.
Fourth, one believes that Amitābha Buddha neither departs nor arrives; thus, I too neither depart nor arrive from the Western Land or this land.
Separated by only the tip of a hair, yet one sees [the Buddha] as soon as one wishes to see. Why is this? Because all Buddhas take the Dharma-nature as their body and land.
Fifth, believe that Amitābha Buddha’s cultivation through successive kalpas until the realization of the fruit does not shift for even a single kṣaṇa;
I too shall not shift for a single kṣaṇa, and my station shall be equal to that of all Buddhas. Why is this? Because time and divisions are but karma.
Because one cannot apprehend karma within the ocean of the Dharma-realm, such faith and understanding is called the initial mind entering the Way,
which has faith in the practice of the pure lands of all Buddhas.

Regarding the two practices of śamatha and vipaśyanā, scholars of both ancient and modern times have extensively established various systems of contemplation based on the *Nirvāṇa*, *Śūraṅgama*, *Avataṃsaka*, and other Vaipulya sūtras;

yet, among these, the Three Contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) of the Tiantai school are the most direct and expedient. They serve as the essential means for revealing the single mind and capture the vital points of all dharmas;
as a path of cultivation, nothing surpasses this. Within the Western (Dharmalaksana) tradition, there are naturally ten [such methods].

Regarding the six correct contemplations (*ṣaḍ-samyak-pratyavekṣā*), each individual contemplation contains these three meanings; therefore, Tiantai’s exegesis of the sutras directly subsumes them under the Three Truths.
The *Miaozongchao* states: "The substance of the three virtues within the nature (*prakṛti*) is the three bodies (*trikāya*) of all Buddhas;
these three virtues and three bodies are my own one mind and three contemplations. If it were not so, then there would be something external to the contemplation."
If the Buddha-realm is not identical to the mind, how can it be called the contemplation of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*) that transcends all relativity?

Furthermore, one may take the three bodies of Amitābha as the Dharma-body and one’s own three contemplations as the Prajñā-wisdom; the accomplishment of these contemplations and the vision of the Buddha are themselves liberation. Just as the letter *i* (𑖀) possesses its three strokes when taken individually yet forms a single character when combined, so too is it with the contemplation of the Buddha.
Since this is the case for the Buddha, the principle that the contemplation of all environments and inhabitants (*shijingshengzheng*) is not a different path follows by extension.

As this has been explained in detail in the *Shuchao* (Commentary on the Sub-commentary), it cannot be fully recounted here. As for Chan Master Wenling, he maintained that a single recitation of the Buddha’s name enters the gate of the three contemplations (*sanguan*).

He taught that when one recites with the three contemplations present—such as when one recites the Buddha’s name once and thereby realizes that the essence of the reciter is empty and the object of recitation is signless—this constitutes the presence of the contemplation of emptiness (*kongguan*);
the Buddha who is the object of recitation is precisely the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which immediately shatters the mind.

This refers to the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vicikitsā-kleśa*). Although one can contemplate that the essence is empty and that which is contemplated is signless (*animitta*), this does not prevent the contemplating subject from being distinct and the object of contemplation from being manifest.

Thus, while contemplating, one maintains the provisional (*saṃvṛti*) perspective; the Buddha who is the object of contemplation is the Reward Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), and through this very mind, one shatters the delusions of "dust and sand" (*reṇu-vāluka*).

Precisely at the moment when both the contemplating subject and the object of contemplation are empty, it is precisely at that time that the contemplating subject and the object of contemplation are manifest. Precisely at the moment when... [the contemplating subject and object are manifest].

When that which is contemplated manifests through the act of contemplation, both the subject and object of contemplation are quiescent; emptiness and the provisional exist in mutual dependence within the persistence of contemplation.
Thus, contemplating the Buddha as the object of thought is to realize the Dharmakāya, which is identical to the mind, thereby shattering ignorance and delusion.

Furthermore, this contemplation of the Buddha takes the three truths as its ultimate cause, purifying those four lands, just as picking up a single mote of dust can transform the great earth into gold.
This is called the inconceivable contemplation gate of the perfect interfusion of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the practitioner of the three and six perfections, the *Awakening of Faith in Mahāyāna* states:

"From the time the Bodhisattva first attains right faith until the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa is about to be completed, a profound understanding of the True Suchness (*tathatā*) dharma manifests before them, such that the practice they cultivate is free from marks."
Because one knows that the essence of the dharma-nature is free from stinginess and greed, one practices in accordance with the *dāna-pāramitā*;

because the dharma-nature is undefiled and free from the faults of the five desires, one practices in accordance with the *śīla-pāramitā*; because the dharma-nature is without suffering and free from anger and affliction, one practices in accordance with the *kṣānti-pāramitā*;
because the dharma-nature is without the characteristics of body or mind and free from indolence, one practices in accordance with the...
Because the *dharmatā* of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) is eternally concentrated and its essence is undisturbed, one practices in accordance with it;

because the essence of the *dharmatā* of the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) is luminous and free from ignorance (*avidyā*), one practices in accordance with it; and because one practices in accordance with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as ultimately empty and does not give rise to a mind of stinginess or greed."
Why is this? Because in ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) there is no stinginess or greed;
since the root of stinginess and greed has been severed, and because the *prajñāpāramitā* is ultimately empty, one never gives rise to a deluded mind. Why is this so?

The Buddha taught that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without giving and without recipient, neither precept nor transgression, and even neither wisdom nor folly. Furthermore, it is said regarding Bodhi...
Although the Bodhisattva does not perceive the act of giving, he gives with a mind purified by emptiness, forming this thought:
"This gift is empty and non-existent; yet, because sentient beings require it, I give. It is like a child who takes earth for gold or silver;
the elder does not see that gold or silver as real, so he gives according to the child's wish, yet in the end, nothing has been given. The remaining five dharmas are also like this.
This is what is called a bodhisattva practicing the six perfections to cultivate a pure land; thus, there are no such distinctions of names or characteristics.
Nevertheless, one does not transcend a single practice that encompasses these six meanings: first, abandoning all miscellaneous thoughts is the practice of giving (*dāna*);
furthermore, binding the mind to the Buddha without dwelling on thoughts of abandonment is the nature of giving. Second, purity within every moment of thought is...

First, practicing the precepts while binding the mind to the Buddha and not seeking the cessation of thought is the precept of nature, for it is the nature-precept (*dharmatā-śīla*). Second, the exhaustion and weakening of worldly thoughts is the practice of patience;
furthermore, binding the mind to the Buddha and not being concerned with suppressing thoughts is the patience of nature, for it is the nature-patience (*dharmatā-kṣānti*).

Third, the non-retrogression of one's resolve is the practice of diligence; furthermore, the single thought-moment of non-attachment to ascetic practices is the diligence of nature, for it is the nature-diligence (*dharmatā-vīrya*).

Fifth, because of progress, one attains the samādhi of mindfulness; this is practicing concentration. Furthermore, every thought-moment is the Buddha, for not craving the flavor of dhyāna is the Great Concentration.
Sixth, one thoroughly understands that the cause of the Buddha is mindfulness itself; while mindful, one is the Buddha. This is practicing wisdom.
Furthermore, mindfulness is fundamentally non-existent and the Buddha is fundamentally non-non-existent; not falling into the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism is the Knowledge of All Modes.
Therefore, the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha can encompass all practices. Why is this? Because mindfulness of the Buddha is a dharma-gate of the one mind;

since there are no practices apart from the mind, it includes them all. Nevertheless, one does not abandon these various practices, for if one were to abandon these practices, one would be abandoning the mind itself.

Fourth, regarding the practitioner of compassionate vows: the ocean of the nature of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is inexhaustible; their offerings are inexhaustible, their precepts and generosity are inexhaustible, and even their benefit to others is inexhaustible.

Just as the ten great vows of Samantabhadra have no end as long as the realm of space and the realm of sentient beings endure, so too shall these vows of mine never come to an end, and my actions of body, speech, and mind shall never grow weary.
It is called the "King of Vows," for there is not a single Buddha who does not accomplish such a King of Vows and realize the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. Thus,
the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu’s *Five Contemplations of the Pure Land* takes the first four— prostration, praise, making vows, and contemplation—
as the "Gate of Accomplishing Merit for Entry," and dedicates [the merit] to all sentient beings afflicted by defilements to uproot them from the mundane world.
Suffering serves as the gateway for accomplishing the merit of transcendence; when a Bodhisattva cultivates the five gates of mindfulness, they swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
An objection is raised: both the Buddha and sentient beings are fundamentally non-existent, as stated in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra:
"The Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings as being like an echo, like a bubble on water, as unsubstantial as a plantain tree, and as fleeting as lightning."
Abiding for a long time like those in the formless realm; form being like the sprout of scorched grain; a bodhisattva who has attained patience regarding greed, anger, and the violation of precepts;
afflictions and habitual tendencies being like what is seen in a dream after one has already awakened—when a bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings as being thus, they are fundamentally empty.
When a bodhisattva makes various vows to benefit living beings, is it not like seeing flowers in the sky with one's own eyes?
The answer is: In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Buddha states that saying "there is no Buddha" therein is for the purpose of destroying attachment to the notion of a Buddha;
it does not mean grasping at the characteristic of a non-Buddha. Therefore, one should know that saying "there are no sentient beings" is for the purpose of destroying the notion of sentient beings;

it does not mean grasping at the characteristic of non-sentient beings. Just as with the term "pure," when a Bodhisattva has performed this contemplation, they say of themselves: "I shall act for the sake of the multitude."
To preach such a Dharma is itself true compassion; it means knowing that a Bodhisattva does not grasp at the mark of a sentient being.
Furthermore, to preach this Dharma is itself the true benefit of beings and the true vow of compassion; there is no separate act of delivering sentient beings.
It is also like the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which says that when a Bodhisattva enters deeply into great compassion, it is like a compassionate father seeing his son who has encountered misfortune.
The child died after being lost (searching for him, he could not be found). His father felt great pity for him, thinking, "This child has died merely because of his empty deception.

The Buddhas likewise know that all phenomena are empty and ultimately unobtainable; yet sentient beings do not know this. Because they do not know it, they become defiled and attached within the midst of empty phenomena.
Due to the causes and conditions of such attachment, they fall into the great hells. For this reason, [the Bodhisattva] enters deeply into great compassion.
Thus, the Buddhas give rise to kindness and exercise compassion precisely because sentient beings are empty and because sentient beings are deceived into entering the cycle of birth and death;

how could there be any principle for them to withdraw their compassionate vows? Therefore, we know that the Bodhisattvas' various means of delivering sentient beings stem from their profound realization of the meaning of the non-existence of sentient beings.
Why is this? Because if one perceives the existence of sentient beings, there is a self, and one's compassion will be inferior; how could this be otherwise?
One who is able to practice such beneficial conduct—as the former masters have said—remains entirely within the gate of self-benefit until reaching the ultimate stage.

From the initial mind of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), through the ten abidings (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), up until the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) just before Buddhahood, even Samantabhadra remains within the gate of benefiting both self and others.
Only upon ascending to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*su-pratibhāsa-bodhi*) after attaining Buddhahood does one [fully enter that state].
Virtue alone is the practice for benefiting others. As the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The fruit of merit is profoundly deep;
there is no one like me who knows its measure of gratitude. Although I have exhausted its limits and depths, it was because my original desire was insatiable that I attained Buddhahood.
Therefore, even now I do not cease; though there is no further merit to be gained, my desire remains."
One must also know that the ocean of the Dharma is boundless and cannot have its depths fathomed by means of measuring rods or wooden poles.

It is like a foolish child who, seeing a pole before a gate, says it reaches halfway to the sky; when calculating the distance from the earth to the heavens, he claims it is no more than two poles high.
The frivolous proliferation of conceptualizations regarding the Buddha-dharma is just like this.
Fifth, regarding those who practice in accordance with the Dharma: within the ocean of the Dharma-realm, the oceans of the bodhisattva practices are likewise immeasurable and boundless.
To apply colors, pigments, or ink to empty space is merely labor in vain; since the Dharma-realm has no tracks or traces, what use are they?

Therefore, the practice of the self-nature of a bodhisattva is neither existent nor non-existent, neither practicing nor not practicing; it is solely that which accords with the self-nature of the Dharma.
Regarding the first practice: although the Bodhisattva brings all sentient beings to ultimate *nirvāṇa* without exception, the realm of sentient beings does not diminish.
It is like puppets on a stage whose laughter and weeping are vividly apparent, yet consist of nothing more than clay and are ultimately empty and non-existent;

this is called the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*). Regarding the second: although the Bodhisattva commits the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), he is free from affliction and anger, reaching the stage of earth.
In the hells there are no defilements of sin; even among animals, there are no faults such as ignorance or arrogance.
It is like a courtesan whose soul departs to follow her lover until she conceives a child, yet her body remains constantly before her parents—this is called the third type of Dharma-practice.
Furthermore, a Bodhisattva may enter meditative absorption with his own body and emerge from it with another body, or enter absorption with one body and emerge with many bodies.

Entering meditative absorption from the body of a sentient being and emerging from absorption from the body of a non-sentient object— like a fierce tiger reviving a corpse to prostrate, dance, and perform as it pleases,
while the corpse itself remains devoid of consciousness— this is called the fourth practice of the Dharma. Furthermore, within the body of a single small sentient being,
the Bodhisattva turns the Great Wheel of Dharma, kindles the Great Torch of Dharma, and thunders the Great Drum of Dharma within the palaces of Māra.
He destroys and causes the great earth to tremble, delivering immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, yet this small sentient being does not perceive it nor know of it;

it is like when the celestial musicians fled into the nostril of a young girl, searching everywhere for them without success, while the girl herself neither perceived nor knew it—this is called the fifth practice of the Dharma. Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva wishes to remain long in the world...
To perform within a single moment of thought what would otherwise take immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of eons,
and then, desiring to dwell in the world for but a short time, to condense those immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of eons into a single moment of thought—
just as a child watching a horse race in a lantern cannot discern its beginning or end despite the vast number of figures— is called "Dharma-practice. This is it.

Therefore, if one realizes such inconceivable practice, within a single thought-moment, the pure lands of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are subsumed therein without exception; this is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of adorning the pure land.
It can be perceived by means of non-conceptual wisdom, but it cannot be fathomed by the calculations of the ordinary mind. Why? Because its self-nature transcends all measures.
Therefore. *Xi-fang-he-lun*, Scroll Six;
*Xi-fang-he-lun*, Scroll Seven.
Seventh, the Gate of Rebirth:
Now, ultimate *nirvāṇa* is exclusively for the Tathāgatas; for the two vehicles, it is a provisional name for the cessation of the attachment to existence and the grasping at emptiness.

Even for Bodhisattvas who have developed true, untainted wisdom and partially shattered ignorance, this is so—how much more so for those of inferior faculties and shallow understanding, who are but a single drop in the great ocean? How could they possibly [attain it] abruptly?

To flaunt wild wisdom and sever the possibility of future existence, taking self-indulgence as play and spiritual cultivation as a fetter—killing oneself and killing others—is no different from ingesting poison.

For example, during the time of the Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who attained the four dhyānas and gave rise to overweening pride, claiming to have attained arhatship and no longer seeking further progress. When his life was about to end, he saw within the four dhyānas...
When the signs of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) appear, one immediately gives rise to false views, saying, "There is no nirvana; the Buddha has deceived me.

Because such evil and perverse thoughts arise, one loses the intermediate state of the fourth *dhyāna* and perceives the signs of the intermediate state of the Avīci Hell. Upon the end of that life, one is reborn in the Avīci Hell.

These cases are like those who, while practicing meditation and observing the precepts, falsely claim realization in a single thought-moment and consequently sink into the black hells. Now, regarding meditation...
People who achieve a small measure of progress consider it sufficient; their minds wander onto deviant paths, and they remain ignorant of how their evil retribution will unfold.

As the ancients said: "If one is not born in the Pure Land, what land can one be born in? The path of the three great kalpas is far and long, and those who enter other gates often suffer retrogression and fall.
For this reason, the holy streams of both past and present all advocate this single gate. Now, I shall briefly indicate six types [of practitioners] therein.
The definitive guide:
first, bodhisattvas born among humans; second, bodhisattvas born in Tuṣita Heaven;
third, bodhisattvas born in the Heaven of Long Life (Ābhāsvara); fourth, bodhisattvas born outside the world-system.
1. Bodhisattvas who, at the time of their first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), are born into the family of the Tathāgata;
2. Bodhisattvas who, having fulfilled the practices of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, are born in the worlds of the ten directions to benefit all sentient beings;
3. Bodhisattvas who are born among human beings, as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: "There are bodhisattvas who, having passed away from among humans, return [to that state]."

Among those born as humans, excluding those who are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), these bodhisattvas have dull faculties and cannot quickly bring the *prajñāpāramitā*, the various *dhāraṇī-mukhas*, and the *samādhi-mukhas* into manifestation.

Indeed, within the human "burning house" (*agnighara*), one is entangled by a hundred forms of suffering; yet when a great bodhisattva dwells therein, they remain untainted and unburdened, like a swan.

When entering water, the water does not wet him. As for those bodhisattvas of lesser capacity who have not deeply planted roots of goodness—advancing a foot only to retreat a fathom—how could they possibly attain the various samādhis?
For example, Śāriputra practiced the bodhisattva path for sixteen hundred kalpas;
when he wished to cross the river of giving, a beggar came and asked for his eyes, and Śāriputra plucked out one eye and gave it to him.
Having attained [supernormal] vision, he spat before Śāriputra and discarded the spittle upon the ground; he then stepped on Śāriputra with his foot.
Śāriputra thought to himself, "It is difficult to deliver such base people as these. It would be better for me to discipline myself and quickly escape from birth and death.
Having reflected thus, he retreated from the path of the Bodhisattva and returned to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Furthermore, it was like a flying seer (*ṛṣi*)...

When the King’s consort touched [the Buddha], his supernatural powers were instantly lost; this was due to the causes from Kāśyapa’s past life, when he used *mṛdvīkā* (jujube) pills mixed with aphrodisiacs to seduce a courtesan.
If even a sage and holy one is thus affected, how much more so those of a beginner's mind?

How could they compare to those who, through a single thought-moment of the Amitābha Samādhi, swiftly manifest their physical form in the Lotus Land to be forever free from desire? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Wisdom that Goes Beyond) states: "The Bodhisattva does not perceive the present..."

The Buddha, knowing that their minds were dull, understood that Bodhisattvas should always remain near the Buddha; for by being near the Buddha, their faculties become sharp and they quickly attain Prajñā.

Furthermore, those two Bodhisattvas who are born in Tuṣita Heaven are all Bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), and it is the rule that such Bodhisattvas are born in Tuṣita.
If those who wish to follow [the Buddha] in descending to be born [in this world] are also born in that place, the *Ten Doubts Treatise* states:
"The Tuṣita Heaven palace is a place where those who have regressed from the desire realm are numerous; furthermore, there are women, which give rise to the various desires of the devas.

The celestial maidens are so exquisite that the devas become infatuated with them and cannot bear to part from them. This is not like the Pure Land of Amitābha, which consists solely of Mahāyāna practitioners as pure and excellent companions."
Because afflictions and evil karma never arise again, one eventually attains the stage of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Thus, when Bodhisattva Siṃhabuddhi was born there to enjoy celestial pleasures, from that time onward he never again saw Maitreya; if even these minor bodhisattvas still cling to the five desires, how much more so must ordinary beings?
Furthermore, according to the *Maitreya-sūtra on the Upper Rebirth*, it is only upon entering right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) that one first attains [this state].
Since there is no further sense of being guided or led by skillful means once born there, one would not even seek rebirth in the Inner Court of Tuṣita;
how much less so in the various heavens of the Desire Realm, which are mere thickets of exquisite sensual desires?
How could anyone, needing a drink, enter a land of burning stones, or seeking to avoid drowning, sink to the bottom of the great ocean?
Regarding the third point—that Bodhisattvas are born among the gods such as the Āyus-mātras—the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"When a Bodhisattva lacks skillful means (*upāya*), they enter the first dhyāna and so forth, even practicing the six pāramitās. One who lacks skillful means, at the time of entering the first dhyāna, does not bring sentient beings to mind;

while dwelling in it or arising from it, they do not bring sentient beings to mind, but merely become attached to the flavor of dhyāna (*dhyānāsvāda*) and are unable to practice in union with the first dhyāna."
Because the bodhisattva’s mind of compassion is thin, the merit of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is meager;

thus, one is led by the retribution of the first dhyāna to be born in the Heaven of Long Life. Those in the Heaven of Long Life reside in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception for eighty thousand great kalpas.
Alternatively, some say that all formless concentrations (ārūpya-samādhi) are collectively termed the "Heaven of Long Life," because they are devoid of [form].

Because their physical forms cannot be transformed, they are incapable of attaining the Way; as they constantly remain in the state of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), some say that the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) is called "long-lived," yet it too is incapable of attaining the Way.

Others say that from the First Dhyāna to the Fourth Dhyāna, with the exception of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), all are called "long-lived," because attachment to flavors and wrong views make it difficult for a wholesome mind to arise, as stated in the Sūtras.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus: "Which is more numerous, the dust on my fingernail or the dust upon the earth? The bhikṣus replied: "The dust upon the earth is exceedingly vast;
it cannot be used as a comparison. The Buddha said: "Those who, having ended their lives in the heavens, are reborn among humans are like the dust on my fingernail;
those who fall into hell are like the dust upon the earth. Why is this? Because they originally set forth the aspiration for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
If one were to accumulate various merits within meditative concentration and only then be reborn among humans to hear the Buddha-dharma,
there would be such faults as those mentioned; however, for one who first resolves to seek birth in a Pure Land, they will constantly hear the Dharma until reaching the stage of non-retrogression—
how could such faults possibly exist?
Regarding the four types of bodhisattvas who are born outside the triple world (*traidhātuka*), there are two kinds:

first, those of the two vehicles and the third kind of bodhisattva who suppress active afflictions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa*), abandon the coarse-and-fine body (*aupapaduka-deha*), and are born outside the world. Because their compassion and wisdom are narrow and inferior, they take no delight in adorning the buddha-fields or benefiting others;
thus, they are rebuked by the Tathāgata. If they do not turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], they will ultimately fail to practice the six perfections and other such deeds.
Regarding Bodhisattvas of the two *dharmakāyas* who do not enter the ocean of Mahāyāna wisdom, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"There are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and are not born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm;
they travel from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field, making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and praising the relics of the Buddhas. Śāriputra... [the text continues].
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, sporting with supernatural powers, travel from one buddha-field to another;
wherever they arrive, there is not even the name of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, let alone those of the two vehicles.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose lifespan is immeasurable wherever they go. (Referring to Nāgārjuna) it is said: "There are two kinds of bodhisattvas."

There are two kinds of bodhisattvas: first, those with birth-bodies (*janmakāya*), and second, those with dharma-bodies (*dharmakāya*). Bodhisattvas with dharma-bodies have severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and attained the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Bodhisattvas with birth-bodies have not severed the fetters; some have abandoned desire and attained five supernormal powers, while others have attained all six.

Those who have attained the six supernormal powers are not born within the three realms; the worlds they reach are all pure according to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and their lifespans are immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya*.
During the *kalpas* of reverence, Bodhisattvas are born there to joyfully accumulate the merits of all Buddhas (referring to the merit of making offerings to the Buddhas).

Therefore, one should know that it is extremely rare for a Bodhisattva to be born there unless they possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). As for ordinary beings who attain rebirth there, it is due to the power of the Buddha and the inconceivable power of their mindfulness;
for within every moment of thought, they are endowed with the six supernormal powers.

When the five bodhisattvas first give rise to the mind [of enlightenment], they are born into the family of the Tathāgata (awakening to the Way of the Tathāgata); these are individuals of the highest capacity for whom fundamental wisdom is shown directly (clearly seeing the Buddha-nature).
At the very moment their initial resolve first arises within the stage of the Ten Abidings, they are identical to the Buddhas.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there is a class of bodhisattvas who, though practicing the six pāramitās for hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, do not yet give birth to the Buddha-family.

This is the provisional designation for a Bodhisattva who, although having seen the Buddha-nature, has not yet manifested the karma of wisdom. The *Jueyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) by Zhangzhe says:

"At the very moment of first generating the mind, one is named as abiding [in the first stage]. These few words below correctly explain its meaning. It clarifies that from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one manifests the gate of fundamental wisdom of emptiness. Ignorance (*avidyā*) begins to cease and wisdom begins to become clear.
Being born into the house of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, it is called "abiding where the Buddhas abide," and thus one attains it.

Recalling the Dharma-gate of the Universal Door of the Wisdom-Light of the Realm of All Buddhas, one thereby perceives the Way, free from distinctions of past, present, and future, or center and periphery.
By passing through the five stages, refining habitual tendencies, and increasing compassion, this is called the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Therefore, it is said that at the very moment of first generating the Bodhicitta, one attains perfect enlightenment; only then can one cultivate the path, as exemplified by Sudhana.

(Citing this as proof that one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) before practicing the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)): He traveled south in search of superior spiritual friends, all of whom said, "I have already set my mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

how then should I learn the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivate the path of a bodhisattva? They did not say that increasing the Buddha-way constitutes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), nor that it is realized through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as being without action or cultivation; rather, they taught only the conduct of a bodhisattva, whereby fundamental wisdom becomes self-evident.

If one does not realize the essence of perfect enlightenment for oneself, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; these are all the karmic retributions of birth and death belonging to humans and devas.

(The following also speaks of the practices of those who have attained right wisdom. It further states that when one awakens the mind in accordance with reality during this present life, one attains right wisdom and, through the practice of contemplation upon the body of segmented existence (*paricchinna-deha*), accomplishes the mind while concurrently cultivating wholesome karma, so that in a future life one enters the body of transformation (*pariṇāma-kāya*).

This present body of segmented existence is the result of past karma; by cultivating contemplation with wisdom in this life, one attains the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and transformations of birth in future lives.
For instance, even those who perform the ten wholesome deeds are born in the heavens and obtain supernatural powers as a karmic retribution;
even great dragons and powerful spirits, despite their afflictions of ignorance and evil karma, still possess such powers—how much more so, then, for one on the Path?

The power of the roots of goodness of benevolence causes the spiritual faculties of wisdom to function (in the application of the mind to Prajñā); yet, by forming a single thought-moment [of aspiration], one may fail to attain the great utility of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) in a future life.
The *Zongjing lu* states: "That a beginner attains Buddhahood does not mean they lack all merits;
as the sutras say, the youth Viśuddhamaṇḍitaka attained [realization] in one lifetime through hearing and being well-impregnated [by the teachings], while another did so in two lifetimes."
Having perfected their practice and realization, they enter the ocean of fruition through three births within a single dependent origination;

yet these three births occur in a single thought-moment, just as a long journey is completed with the first step. However, this arrival at the first step does not mean that subsequent steps are unnecessary.
Thus, it is clear that this youth’s entry into the ocean of fruition was not achieved without having planted roots of goodness over a long period. Question: Since he has practiced for so long...

Question: How can it be said that one attains [enlightenment] in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*)? Answer: One who has long cultivated roots of goodness is already encompassed within the teachings of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).
By entering the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) from the Three Vehicles, the initial cultivation is perfected in that very single thought-moment. As the Sūtra says:

"At the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one immediately becomes a Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). It is like various rivers entering the ocean; as soon as a single drop enters, it is said to pervade the entire great sea.
Without beginning and without end, it is like the waters of the myriad rivers: even their extreme depths cannot equal a single drop that enters the great ocean.

This is just as the cultivation of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* within the Three Vehicles does not equal a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-ksana*) in the One Vehicle. Furthermore, at this time, kalpas are not fixed;
a single thought-moment may be immeasurable kalpas, as in the Ten Mysterious Gates where time and place are unimpeded. Moreover, this is clearly elucidated in the Mahāyāna.

There are two ways in which one attains Buddhahood in a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*): first, by integrating all conditions to enter into the true nature (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*), wherein there is neither increase nor decrease;

this clarifies attaining Buddhahood in a single thought-moment. Second, when the practice of the paths is just completed, taking that final thought-moment as "attaining Buddhahood in a single thought-moment";

this is like a person traveling a long distance who considers the final step to be their arrival. As for the clarification of attaining Buddhahood in a single thought-moment according to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), it is the same as in the Mahāyāna.
Taking the subsequent single thought-moment of attaining Buddhahood, one immediately enters the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This subsequent [moment] is itself the initial [moment]; why?

Because cause and effect are mutually identical and correspond simultaneously. Thus, although one attains Buddhahood in a single thought-moment, this is equivalent to the rank of a newly arisen Buddha (*abhinavotpanna-buddha*) and does not yet possess ultimate perfection;
therefore, there remain distinctions of depth and shallowness, like a person who has just stepped out of a door versus one who has been gone for a long time.
Although those who travel to other lands are equally situated in the midst of space, there are distinctions between the distant and the near;

for this reason, it is said that each of the five stages—such as the ten faiths and the ten abodes—achieves Buddhahood, while their relative shallowness or depth is further distinguished. One must reflect well upon this point.
If one understands the words of these two Great Beings, then one will know that practitioners who have attained realization through the Chan gate must not abandon any of the various practices.
This grinds away the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless time. Indeed, dwelling in this turbid and evil world, one step forward is countered by ten thousand steps back;
if one does not draw near to the Buddha, defilements and impurities will converge, and how could practice ever be accomplished?

It was when Sudhana first resolved his mind to realize the Way that the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī instructed him in the Dharma-gate of recollecting all Buddhas, and after he entered the tower of Maitreya, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva [further guided him].
To give rise to the ten great kings of vows and guide one’s rebirth in Sukhāvatī is the paradigm for entering the Way taught by all Tathāgatas.
This is the gateway to the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-tathatā-dharmadhātu*) as expounded in the *Avataṃsaka*, which differs from other teachings that possess both provisional and ultimate aspects.

If one does not believe in this sutra, they are a *icchantika*—one who has severed the roots of goodness—even if Śākyamuni were to praise them, Samantabhadra were to exhort them, and Maitreya were to bear witness.
"What can one do about it? It is already so.
As for the six bodhisattvas who have fulfilled their practice over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and are born in the worlds of the ten directions to benefit all sentient beings:
because the merits of these bodhisattvas are fully perfected, they naturally possess inconceivable karma that can manifest throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings.

The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "A Bodhisattva who has realized the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is able, in a single thought-moment, to reach all worlds throughout the ten directions without exception to make offerings to the Buddhas and request them to turn the wheel of Dharma. This is solely for the purpose of guiding and benefiting sentient beings, and does not rely on written words.

Alternatively, he may manifest the swift attainment of perfect enlightenment by transcending the stages (*bhūmi*) for the sake of those sentient beings who are timid; or he may say, 'I [have attained it] in the absence of...'"
For the sake of sentient beings who are indolent, it is taught that after immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas one shall attain Buddhahood;

yet, in reality, for those of the Bodhisattva lineage whose roots and so forth are equal, their initial resolve is equal, what they realize is equal, and there is no dharma by which one may surpass another, because all Bodhisattvas pass through three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The World-Honored One Śākyamuni, from the past..."
From Śākyamuni Buddha back to Śikhin Buddha constitutes the first asaṃkhyeya; from Śikhin Buddha until the time of receiving the prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha constitutes the second asaṃkhyeya;
and from Dīpaṃkara Buddha back to Vipaśyin Buddha constitutes the third asaṃkhyeya.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* describes these three asaṃkhyeya kalpas as the period for practicing the six pāramitās and planting the seeds during one hundred kalpas.
Having first cultivated the causes for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), one subsequently attains the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*).

According to the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) school, one passes through the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*), completes the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* at the fulfillment of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), and reaches the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* from the eighth stage up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);

only then does one attain the ultimate Dharma-body. An objection is raised: All the treatises of the Elder [Nāgārjuna] state that these do not depart from a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*) throughout the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. How can you maintain this [position]?
Question: "The fixed eons are eternally at variance with the primary meaning. Answer: "The Elder merely says that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are fundamentally empty;

the essence of time cannot be apprehended. This does not mean that time does not exist. It is like saying that a person’s eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body—these six roots currently present—are fundamentally non-existent.
This is not to say that the six roots are abolished by declaring them 'non-existent. It is like a child who, seeing the moon in the water, conceives a mind of attachment."
One may cling to the grasping of desire, yet it cannot be obtained. The wise teach that while this can be seen with the eyes, it cannot be grasped by the hand;
thus, one destroys what is graspable, but not what is visible. The activities of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the three periods of time are likewise so:
although everything is unobtainable, it is not that there is no practice. For instance, both the two great Bodhisattvas, Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghoṣa, were such.
How could the patriarchs who transmitted the robe in the Chan school ever deceive themselves or others, leading later generations astray?
One must realize that the matter of birth and death is of great importance; it cannot be escaped through mere fragmentary knowledge or half-measured practice. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"There are bodhisattvas of sharp faculties and firm resolve who, even before they have formally resolved their minds for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), have long since accumulated immeasurable merit and wisdom. Such persons encounter..."
Upon hearing this Mahāyāna Dharma, the Buddha gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (the lower text’s description of supernormal powers serves as a direct analogy for this).
He immediately practiced the six *pāramitās*, entered the stage of a bodhisattva, and attained the level of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression). Why is this so?

Because he had previously accumulated immeasurable merit, possessed sharp faculties, and maintained a firm mind; having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, it was as if someone traveling a great distance who might ride upon a vehicle.

Some departed on sheep, some departed on horseback, and some departed by means of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Those who rode sheep arrived after a long time; those who rode horses were somewhat faster;
and those who traveled by supernatural powers arrived in the mere space of a single thought-moment (*cittotpāda*).

Thus, one must not say that they arrived in the interval of a single thought-moment—how could it be otherwise? The nature of supernatural power is such that one should not give rise to doubt. The Bodhisattva is also like this.
At the moment one generates the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one enters the rank of a bodhisattva.
Although a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment may initially have a virtuous mind that later becomes mixed with various evils, they occasionally give rise to the thought:
"I seek the Buddha-way and dedicate all merits toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Such a person, after a long period of immeasurable time...
Whether an *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa is reached or not depends on whether the causes and conditions of merit from previous lives were meager and one’s faculties dull with an unstable mind—
like one riding a sheep. Conversely, if there was even a small amount of merit in a previous life,
and one possesses sharp faculties and resolves the mind to gradually practice the six *pāramitās* for three, ten, or a hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is like a rider on horseback who must necessarily reach a destination; this third vehicle, that of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), is as described above.
One knows that gradual cultivation and sudden realization are each different. Since there is no such thing as reaching the Buddha-stage abruptly, the masters of old said:
"Though one may equal the Buddha's awakening, if one has not yet attained the ultimate fruit, it is not the final consummation."
Therefore, those who have attained awakening must resolutely seek rebirth in the Pure Land and practice according to the Dharma to avoid falling back;
only when the power of patience has become firm should they enter the world to benefit sentient beings, for this constitutes the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood.
Compendium of the Western Regions, Volume Seven;
Compendium of the Western Regions, Volume Eight:
Chapter Eight, The Gate of the Net of Views.
Indeed, all deluded sentiments arise based on various views; to tread upon them is like entering a dense forest, and to be submerged in them is like drowning in a scorching sea.
It is like a silkworm spinning its cocoon—the very dwelling place becomes the cause of its own bondage—or like a moth rushing toward a lamp, relying on the light as the basis for its own destruction.
Therefore, the predecessors said: "Practice arises when conceptual understanding ceases. For this reason, before one approaches the chamber of the Sages, [one must first...]

Entering the gate of Samantabhadra and wishing to cultivate the primary cause, one must first sever the net of false views. Herein, based on the errors and fallacies of various schools, I shall briefly divide this into ten points.
There is no dharma to be abandoned; such a view must be rebuked. A wanderer who has left his home is accustomed to pitying those who are wayfarers;
a cold scholar who failed the examinations fully understands the bitterness of being at a dead end. May you fortunately follow the words of the Buddha and not rely upon Māra.
The teachings [warn against] six fallacies: first, the fallacy of nihilism; second, the fallacy of cowardice and inferiority; third, the fallacy of following mere words;
fourth, the fallacy of wild license; fifth, the fallacy of fragmentation; and sixth, the fallacy of deluded emptiness.
7. Falling into following conditions; 8. Falling into mind-only; 9. Falling into sudden enlightenment;
10. Falling into perfect reality.
Regarding the first, falling into annihilationism, there are two types: first, various Confucian scholars who are stuck on the present body and doubt that the future will cease to exist.

To eliminate the doubts of those who have newly resolved to seek enlightenment and those learners who cling to the mark of emptiness—fearing that all things are annihilated—such as those who do not even believe in rebirth, let alone in the Pure Land and other such matters, I shall now provide a brief explanation. First, regarding the "Confucian scholars" and others:
in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Buddha said to King Prasenajit, "Now you yourself lament that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled."

"If your face is certainly more wrinkled than it was in childhood, then when you now look at this Ganges River, is there any difference between this seeing and the seeing that looked at the river in your childhood—any distinction of youth or old age?
The King replied, "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face is wrinkled, the essence of this seeing-nature has never been wrinkled.
That which is wrinkled undergoes change; that which is not wrinkled does not change. That which changes is subject to extinction."
That which is unchanging is fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing; how could one undergo birth and death therein?
And yet you speak of this body being utterly extinguished after death. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "When a person dies, they return to extinction. There are three kinds of extinction:
first, being burned by fire until reduced to ashes; second, being eaten by insects until reduced to dung; and third, ultimately returning to the earth. Now we see only their extinction."
If one sees that there are further beings who receive a subsequent body, yet because they are not seen [at present], one concludes they do not exist, the answer is:
if you claim that when the body perishes there is nothing more, how can there be the sorrow, joy, fear, and so forth practiced by sentient beings in previous lives?
For instance, when a small child is born, it may cry or laugh; because of its prior practice of sorrow and joy, it experiences sorrow now even without anyone teaching it.

The continuity of joy at birth is like that of a calf, which knows how to seek milk upon being born; or like pigs, sheep, and other such animals, which soon after birth know the union of male and female.
Furthermore, among siblings born of the same parents, there are differences in beauty and ugliness, wealth and poverty, intelligence and dullness;
these variations would not exist if there were no causal conditions from previous lives. Such are the various causes and conditions.
Regarding the knowledge that there is a future life: furthermore, you previously stated that you do not see a separate "goer" within the human body;

however, it is not only the faculty of sight that can perceive what is within the body. Each of the six sense organs has its own specific objects of cognition: there are things that can be heard, smelled, tasted, touched, and known.
If even the audible phenomena cannot be seen, how much less so those things that must be known? There is birth and there is death.
The Dharma can both be seen and known; however, because you possess only the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), you do not see it.

One who possesses the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) can see it clearly, just as one sees a person entering or leaving a room. When this body is abandoned and one reaches a subsequent body, it is likewise so.

If the fleshly eye were able to see [the Dharma], what need would there be to seek the divine eye? If that were the case, then between the foolish and the noble, there would be no distinction regarding the fleshly and divine eyes.
To differ from you [by viewing] that one is the same as an animal—how could such a view enable one to perceive what is knowable regarding future lives?
Although there is no coming or going when a person dies and is reborn, because afflictions are not yet exhausted, the continuity of body, mind, and feelings arises again.
The body, mind, and feelings create karma; although this karma does not travel to a future life, through these causes and conditions, one is born again and undergoes subsequent experience.

The retribution of the world is like poison placed in milk: the milk transforms into curd, and the curd transforms into ghee. Yet the milk is not the curd or the ghee, nor are the curd and the ghee the milk;
although the milk and the curd undergo transformation, they all contain the poison. This body is also like this:

by reason of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the present life, the five aggregates of a future life arise again. Because the continuity of karmic actions is not different, one receives [retribution].
The retribution of karma is like a winter tree: although it has not yet produced flowers, leaves, or fruit, when it encounters the proper season, they emerge in succession.
For this reason, one knows that death and birth exist. Furthermore, there are those in the present life who possess the knowledge of past lives (*jātismara*).
It is like a person who travels in a dream and becomes exhausted; upon waking and lying down again, they remember the path they traversed. Moreover, all noble ones (*ārya*) internally...
The external scriptures all state that in future lives—and furthermore, even in this present life—the arising of unwholesome states leads to the heavy production of anger, envy, doubt, and regret.
Because of these internal afflictions, the body becomes withered and the complexion loses its luster; one is thus harmed by evil and unwholesome states.
How much more so when physical and verbal actions are incited? If, however, wholesome states arise through the causal conditions of pure faith and karma, [the result is the opposite].
When the mind is pure, one attains wisdom that accords with reality; the mind then becomes joyful, the body becomes light and supple, and the complexion becomes harmonious and serene.

Because there are causes and conditions for suffering and pleasure, there exist the wholesome and the unwholesome. Since there are certainly wholesome and unwholesome deeds in this present life, one should know that there must necessarily be a future world.
Although sentient beings do not see it with their physical eyes, they give rise to false doubts because their wisdom is shallow. Nevertheless—
The merit performed through virtuous deeds is shallow and slight, like a physician who treats a king’s illness; while the king secretly builds a residence for him, the physician is unaware of it.
Upon returning and seeing it, he then regrets not having applied his mind and exerted his full effort in treating the king.
Furthermore, because the sages state that present realities are trustworthy, their accounts of future matters are likewise all to be trusted. As it is said:
When a person travels at night on a perilous path, they will follow along if a guide extends a hand to them, for they know the guide is trustworthy.
By means of inference (*anumāna*) and the words of the sages, one can know that a future life definitely exists.

Because you possess only physical eyes, your heavy karmic offenses, and your feeble power of inference, and because you lack divine vision (*divyacakṣus*), you yourself have no wisdom and do not believe the words of the sages; how then can you know [that there is a future life]? (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* concludes here. It is as was declared regarding what occurs after the body perishes.
If the words of the Sages are obscure and hidden, they speak of ghosts and spirits; their virtue is so magnificent that they clearly expound upon the Way.
King Wu and the Duke of Zhou were consummate in filial piety, which rested solely on recognizing the nature and conditions of ghosts and spirits, and treating the dead as one treats the living.

Yet Master Kǎo-xīng (Zhu Xi) has deliberately provided a convoluted explanation, reducing it to the two qi (primordial energies). How can he dare to misrepresent the former sages and cast doubt upon those who come after? Furthermore, regarding the unofficial histories and folk records...

The histories need not be discussed further: Peng Sheng becoming a boar, Bo You becoming a malevolent spirit, Liu Chong becoming the King of Zhexu, and Jiang Ji’s son seeking office from the Magistrate of Taishan—these are matters of the official histories (*zhengshi*).
The *Xuan-niao* giving birth to the Shang dynasty and Emperor Wu initiating the Zhou—these are matters of the canonical classics (*zhengjing*).
A magpie transforming into a clam, a field mouse transforming into a quail, and a hawk transforming into a dove—these are matters of the official edicts (*zhengling*).

How much can a single atom of consciousness know? To harbor resentment toward the vastness of the ocean like a frog, or to attempt to obscure the sunlight with a firefly—such acts of insulting the sages and profaning Heaven—what punishment should one expect to receive?
Furthermore, those who speak (referring to the Confucian scholars) constantly claim that what is not experienced by humans or that which contradicts their principles is unworthy of trust;
yet they fail to realize that the movements of the sun and moon, as well as the orbits of the five planets, are not things experienced by humans.
One can experience this: Heaven does not come here, nor does this person go there; how then can one infer that all things are verified?
Furthermore, what makes Heaven high and what makes Earth low? Why does the wind arise and why do the clouds move?

What causes spring to bring life and autumn to bring death? What principle can be relied upon here? The root within the womb is devoid of consciousness, yet it revolves; this is called "transformation."
That a mother’s milk flows forth without cause—what principle can be relied upon for this?
From the minute down to a single hair, a speck of dust, a blade of grass, or a tree—if there were even so much as a hair’s breadth of a principle to rely upon, I would gladly point it out for you.

However, since it is merely a matter of common perception, it is "constant" only to that perception; yet even this common perception is itself devoid of reason. Therefore, one should not [rely upon it].

Because one does not see [the cause], doubt arises regarding rebirth. There are two explanations concerning the path of learning (it is said that "the path of learning" refers to those superior Confucian scholars who have not yet mastered the Way).

Regarding those who cling to the mark of emptiness, the treatise says: When a student hears the teaching of emptiness, they conceive doubt within the causes and conditions of karma in birth-and-death (these three phrases collectively quote their words).

If all dharmas are ultimately empty—without coming or going, without exiting or entering (the following is the actual refutation; it should say: "If all dharmas were truly empty, then how could..."). How can there be birth after death? Even the phenomena currently seen before one's eyes should not [be perceived as real].
How much more so after death, when one is reborn in another place! Within the Buddha-dharma, all phenomena (*dharma*) are ultimately empty, yet they are not annihilated;
though the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) continues in succession, it is not eternal.

Although the causes and conditions of karma over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed away, they can still produce retributive fruits without being extinguished. This is subtle, wondrous, and difficult to understand. If...
If all phenomena were entirely empty, the Buddha would not have spoken of rebirth; how could there be a wise person who asserts such a contradiction between what precedes and what follows?

If the characteristics of birth and death truly existed, why would he say that all phenomena are ultimately empty? It is solely for the purpose of eliminating attachment to phenomena, as well as wrong views and perversions, that he speaks of ultimate emptiness;
it is not for the sake of negating future bodies, nor for the sake of obstructing the causes of sinful karma.
For this reason, it is said that one is born into the various Buddha-dharmas without attachment;

one does not attach to existence, nor does one attach to non-existence, nor does one attach to both existence and non-existence, nor does one attach to neither existence nor non-existence. One does not even attach to non-attachment.

For such a person, no challenge can be found—just as when one strikes empty space with a sword, nothing is wounded. This is the characteristic of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). Ultimate emptiness does not obstruct birth and death.
Because this is due to the causal conditions of karma, it is said that those who harbor such doubts regarding rebirth are very shallow;

those with even a slight understanding are able to sever them. Since worldly people most frequently hold this view, it is refuted first, as it constitutes the foremost obstacle for those seeking rebirth.

Second, regarding those who fall through cowardice and inferiority, there are four types of doubt: first, the density of habitual tendencies toward doubt; second, the weakness of the power of contemplation; third, the distance of myriad *koṭis* of lands;

and fourth, the density of habitual tendencies toward doubt. As for the density of habitual tendencies toward doubt: ordinary beings know only the power of karma but do not know that the nature of karma is empty.
Therefore, if the nature of the karma of sentient beings were substantial, even the entirety of the realm of empty space would have no room to contain it.
It is like black clouds obscuring the sky; when the wind arrives, they are extinguished. If the clouds were substantial, even the wind could not disperse them.

The sky is a metaphor for the *dharmatā* (intrinsic nature), the black clouds for karma, and mindfulness of the Buddha for the wind. Furthermore, the power and function of the nature of karma are identical to the power and function of the *dharmatā*;
yet, because of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), this spiritual power does not manifest. As it says: "When Ucchuṣma heard the King of Empty Space Buddha speak much..."

The lustful person becomes a mass of fierce fire; yet later, when one universally contemplates the four limbs, the hundred bones, and all sensations of cold and warmth, the spiritual light condenses within, transforming the many lustful minds into the fire of wisdom.

Since they are both equally the affliction of heat—wherein lust becomes a great mass of fire and its cessation becomes a great jewel-flame—if the nature of lust were real, how could it be that within this [cessation] one attains [wisdom]?
Because of this samādhi, when delusion is formed, one dwells in the prison of the womb; when thought is formed, one immediately enters the lotus calyx.

Since the nature of the womb is identical to the nature of transformation, it does not come from without—just as clarity within turbid water does not come from without. Second, regarding those whose power of doubting thought is slight:
sentient beings are ignorant and deluded, believing in the existence of formal karmic actions while having great disbelief in formless thought.
The power [of mindfulness] is especially great. Why? Because the power of mindfulness is the root of all karmic actions; no undertaking can be accomplished without mindfulness.

For example, when a person commits a transgression, if it was done unintentionally, a heavy offense receives a light retribution; if it was done intentionally, the opposite occurs. This is because the power of mindfulness is so weighty.

It is like when a person is in a state of neutral indifference (*avyākṛta*); even if they are reminded by being told directly in the ear or instructed face-to-face regarding vulgar worldly matters, they still do not remember them.
When the mind is focused, even matters of various kinds that are difficult to record, once they enter the faculty of hearing, are remembered and held fast for a lifetime without being forgotten;

this is because the power of mindfulness is firm. Su Zizhan said: "The Buddha fills the ten directions with his great perfect enlightenment, yet I, through my inverted thoughts, come and go within the cycle of birth and death.
How can I attain rebirth in the Pure Land in a single thought? I have composed [this verse] in response.
The karma of beginningless time originates from a single thought; since it arises from a single thought, it likewise ceases with a single thought.
At the point where arising and ceasing are utterly extinguished, I and the Buddha are identical—like water poured into the sea, or like a bellows being blown by the wind.
Even a Great Sage’s wisdom cannot distinguish between them. The *Jingtu ji* (Record of the Pure Land) states decisively that what is most urgent for a person is the direction of their thoughts.

Just as water inevitably flows to the sea, fire inevitably burns upward, a sharp blade inevitably causes injury, and a poisonous drug inevitably kills—none of these fail to take effect—so too is the mindfulness of the Buddha.

It is like the man of lust who, because his lustful thoughts were so firm, was transformed into a fierce flame that spread and consumed a temple; it is also like the visualization practiced by the youth Candraprabha.
Because of the water, when the disciple peered into the room, he saw only clear water.

Furthermore, when the monk Bhāviveka debated with a non-Buddhist, the non-Buddhist stubbornly clung to his own views and suddenly transformed into stone; while Bhāviveka continued to write down the items of the discussion upon the stone, he went to look at it the next day and found that there was also a response written there.
After a long time, it suddenly shattered of its own accord, and a roaring sound echoed through the air. This is [the story].

All these [powers] arise from the firm and fierce power of mindfulness; how could it be that through the transformation of causes and conditions, one recollects the Buddha yet the Buddha does not appear?
One should know that the power of mindfulness is the king among all dharmas. It is like the great warrior Mahānagna: when he is enraged, a wound inevitably appears upon his forehead;
as long as that wound has not yet healed, no one throughout Jambudvīpa can withstand him. Therefore, [the power of mindfulness is supreme]. Third.
Those who doubt that ten million billion lands are distant are ordinary beings who cling to the fixed notion of ten trillion lands;
they think that even with swift horses or rapid sails, one cannot travel a thousand li in a single day—how then could one be born in such a place in a single *kṣaṇa*?

They fail to consider whether the distance of the land arises from the calculations of the body of segmented birth (*paricchinna-śarīra*) or from the perspective of the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). Is this one who attains rebirth there still a body of segmented birth?
Is this the mind that universally encompasses and contains? If it were the segmented body, since the body is a dull material substance, how could it arise?
If it were the mind, the mind pervades the entire universe; since the Pure Land is originally within the mind, how could there be coming and going?
It is like a person in Chang’an who longs for their hometown—whether it be Min or Dian—it arrives as soon as the thought arises; how could there be any travel distance? Furthermore...
It is like a person in a dream whose body remains on the bed while the mind, intellect, and consciousness travel everywhere to other lands. The Layman Wugong said:

"That the Land of Ultimate Bliss, though ten thousand billion *kṣetras* away from here, can be reached in the mere instant of an ordinary person's death, is because the fundamental nature of one's own mind is wondrous.
Therefore, the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* says: "You have not yet understood that all floating dust-like phenomena are illusory transformations."
Arising in one place and ceasing in another according to the conjunction of causes and conditions, they exist falsely; when causes and conditions separate, they are falsely called "extinguished.
By this reasoning, at the moment of death, because defiled and turbid conditions depart, the Saha world is illusorily extinguished in its very place;
because pure conditions conjoin, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is illusorily born in its very place. Between this extinction and that birth, there is no interval.
How could one even speak of moments regarding the state of his hair and complexion? In my home village, there was once a man who could summon a *jixian* (spirit medium);
this *jixian* was none other than his own elder brother. Later, when he went to the capital to take the imperial examinations, my brother and others sought his divination.

Fearing that the distance was too great for him to travel, the man had no choice but to write talismans and recite incantations; in a short while, [the spirit] arrived. Such phenomena are bound by karma.

If it is this swift even in such [ordinary] matters, how much more so when relying on the inconceivable power of mindfulness and the merit of Amitābha’s original vows—like setting sail with the current, what obstacles or difficulties could there be? Therefore, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha should dispel these three doubts;
if they are not dispelled, it is because their habitual attachments are truly thick, their power of mindfulness is truly slight, and their [past offenses] are truly as many as one hundred thousand.
Cheng Yuanshu’s view is like a person wishing to leave their house who locks their own bolt; this is because they do not wish to go out, not because there is no door through which to pass.
