Third, regarding falling into the trap of words: the Sixth Patriarch said that while people in the East commit sins, those in the West recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth there.

When people commit sins yet practice *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) seeking rebirth in a certain land, Master Pang said: "To speak of Buddha-lands in terms of spatial direction is ten thousand *li* away; the great ocean stretches boundlessly, and as soon as one moves, black winds arise. Because of this, a class of ignorant people transmits the empty and echoes the sound, claiming that the Pure Land is not worth cultivating. To obstruct themselves and others—this is truly pitiable. As for the discussion [of this matter]: [The following is the continuation of the text: "Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Visualization of the Infinite Life* states: 'If there are sentient beings who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and, with a sincere heart, desire to be born in his land, even if they have committed the five grave offenses or the ten evil deeds, provided they do not slander the Dharma, at the moment of death they shall see the Buddha and be born in his land. This is because the Buddha’s power is inconceivable and his vows are unfathomable. How could it be that those who recite the Buddha’s name would not be reborn there?

It is only because people harbor doubts and lack faith that they fail to attain birth. Therefore, one should simply believe and recite with single-minded devotion; there is no need for further deliberation. If one still harbors doubts while reciting, it is like a person crossing a river who, though they have reached the middle, still fears they will drown. Such a person will surely perish. Thus, if you wish to be born in the Pure Land, you must abandon all doubt and recite with unwavering resolve."
In the proclamation of the Zen school, one does not even say that there is a Buddha, let alone a Buddha-land.

This is because it seeks to shatter appearances and clarify the mind, cutting through both right and wrong like a sharp blade; if you grasp it, you will cut your hand. How could the vajra-thorn ever be ordinary daily fare?
Furthermore, such phrases abound within the Zen school; if one were to cling to each and every one of them, Śākyamuni would [be lost].
Will you, my son, emerge into the world to feed the dog of Yunmen with the truth? Furthermore, an ancient worthy asked, "What is the Buddha? and replied, "A dried-up shit-stick.
If this were truly so, then whenever one sees a dung-cart, a dung-litter, or a latrine, one ought to prostrate and make offerings to each and every one of them.
The *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* states that the Western Land is ten thousand billion lands away from here, while the *Platform Sūtra* speaks of ten thousand [lands].
The statement that "eight thousand [yojanas]" refers to the five regions of India as being the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) is nearly correct;
it likely arose because the Sixth Patriarch had not yet read the Tripitaka and, upon hearing people speak of the West, assumed it referred to the five regions of India.

In the teachings, it is clearly stated that in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the three poisons do not arise and one attains non-retrogression; yet now you say that one must travel to the West to create [merit].

That those with transgressions seek rebirth in a particular land is yet another proof of this. However, within the Chan school, such expressions regarding a single lifetime are exceedingly numerous and need not be further debated.

Alas! If a student of the Way can truly achieve sudden awakening and sudden cultivation, such that their understanding and practice correspond, they will be like the Sixth Patriarch casting gold into the Han River or like the Elder Pang, who played freely amidst birth and death; even if they do not seek rebirth, what does it matter?

This is harmful to one's life! Those who fall into the four types of madness and indulgence are demonic followers who exclusively pursue wild wisdom and refuse to uphold the precepts or engage in cultivation.

They perversely cite similar-sounding phrases from the sutras—such as "afflictions are themselves bodhi" or "lust, anger, and delusion are themselves the Brahma-conduct"—and based on these words, they give rise to interpretations;
based on these interpretations, they unleash poison. The results are exactly as described: Kāśyapa attained awakening through this.

The Way should involve intimacy with the "Precious Woman" (the Buddha), yet why would Ānanda enter a brothel? Why did the Sixth Patriarch initially follow hunters before he had even received the precepts?

Why, then, suffer over merely eating vegetables grown near meat? The Sūtra says: "If there is not even non-killing, non-stealing, and non-lust, how much less could there be acts of killing, stealing, or lust?
How could one hear people disparaging agarwood incense and immediately claim that one ought to [use it]?
Regarding those who dwell in latrines: Formerly, in the Five Indias, there was a monk named Dharmadatta who possessed eloquence and wisdom. He served the Venerable Siṃha as his teacher.

The Venerable One, knowing that Dharmadatta had attained realization, praised him before the assembly. However, when it came to the transmission of the Dharma and the succession to the Patriarchate, the Venerable One conferred it upon Vasubandhu.
Dharmadatta felt resentment in his heart and said, "The Venerable One surely knows me deeply; for what reason [did he do this]?"
When he succeeded to the throne, he did not receive formal investiture. One day, while walking alone across water, he saw a woman washing her feet and exposing them;

she rubbed them, and Mudgala thought to himself, "How white and smooth these shanks are! Suddenly, the Venerable One appeared at his side and asked, "Can the mind of this day be granted the position of the Patriarch?
Thereupon, Mudgala composed his thoughts, prostrated at the Venerable One's feet, and sought refuge, immediately undertaking the precept against sexual misconduct as the first of his other practices.
One may cite the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which states: "Because neither transgression nor non-transgression can be apprehended, one should fulfill the Śīla-pāramitā.
The commentary explains that "neither transgression nor non-transgression can be apprehended" does not mean they cannot be apprehended due to wrong views or a coarse mind;

rather, it means that because the Bodhisattva has deeply penetrated the characteristics of all phenomena and practices the Samādhi of Emptiness, observing with the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), transgression cannot be apprehended as a transgression.

Without cause, neither non-offense nor offense can be established. If a person is greedily attached to the view that there is no offense, they will look down upon those who break the precepts while feeling love and respect for those who uphold them.
Such adherence to the precepts is called a causal condition for generating offenses; it is not called being complete. Thus we know that abiding in the precepts is itself a violation;
how much more so is it when one abandons and reviles the precepts? This is what is called the beginning of grasping at the precepts.
The various great sūtras on upholding the precepts state that "the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is unattainable," and so forth; all such passages have this very meaning. Yongming said:

one universally repents on behalf of all sentient beings of the ten directions throughout the past, present, and future.
If one can perform such true repentance, all obstacles will be completely eliminated, and without leaving the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one shall behold the Buddhas.
Regarding the six pure vows, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: When bodhisattvas see that the worlds of various Buddhas are immeasurably adorned and purified, they give rise to various vows.
Seeing Buddha-worlds where there is no suffering whatsoever, even to the point that the names of the three evil realms do not exist, the bodhisattvas, having seen this, make their own vow, saying:
"When I become a Buddha, may my world be free from all suffering, even to the point that [the three evil realms] do not exist."

The names of the three evil realms shall likewise be so; there shall be Buddha-worlds adorned with the seven treasures, where pure light shines constantly day and night, and where there are neither sun nor moon.
Then he makes this vow: "When I become a Buddha, my world shall always possess such majestic, pure light, just as these worlds do.
There shall also be Buddha-worlds where all sentient beings practice the ten virtuous deeds.
There were robes of great wisdom and food and drink that arrived as soon as they were thought of; he then made this vow:
"When I become a Buddha, the sentient beings in my world shall likewise have such robes, food, and drink.

There was a Buddha-world consisting entirely of bodhisattvas, whose physical bodies were like those of a Buddha, possessing the thirty-two marks and with radiance shining forth everywhere, such that there were not even śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Even among those named Pratyekabuddhas, there are no women; all practice the profound and wondrous Buddha-way, traveling throughout the ten directions to teach and transform all beings.
They then make this vow: "When I become a Buddha, the sentient beings in my world shall also be like this.
Such various adornments and purities of immeasurable Buddha-worlds as these—may they all be attained. For this reason, it is so named.
"May I receive the immeasurable worlds of all Buddhas. He asked: "If the practices and deeds of Bodhisattvas are pure, they naturally obtain pure retribution;
why must one necessarily establish vows before attaining them? It is like a farmer who obtains grain—does he wait for a vow? He replied:
"When performing merit, if there is no vow, there is nothing to mark it out. The vow acts as a guide and driver, enabling one to achieve results. For example:"

It is like melting gold, which takes form according to the artisan; the gold itself has no fixed shape. As the Buddha has taught, there are those who cultivate the merit of small-scale giving and the merit of minor precepts, yet remain ignorant of the methods of dhyāna.
Upon hearing that among humans there are those with wealth and joy, or hearing of the heavens of the desire realm and the form realm, they form a longing for them.
After their lives end, each is reborn therein. The Bodhisattva also practices in this same way.
One attains the purification of the world only after first making the vow; for this reason, one knows that through the power of the vow one receives superior fruits.
Furthermore, the task of adorning the Buddha-field is so great that it cannot be accomplished by individual merit alone; it necessarily requires the power of the vow.
For example, although the strength of an ox can pull a cart, it must rely on a driver to reach its destination. The vow to purify the world is likewise.
This merit is like the ox, while the vow is like the driver. He asked: "If one does not make a vow, will one not obtain merit? He replied:
"Although merit may be obtained [without a vow], it is not as it would be with a vow. A vow can assist merit; by constantly recollecting what has been practiced, merit increases.
For this reason, those who cultivate a pure buddha-field should make great vows. First, they do not do so for the sake of becoming a field of merit."
First, one should vow that for the sake of providing shelter for all sentient beings, one shall be born in the Pure Land;
second, one should not do so for the sake of kinsmen, but rather vow that for the sake of entering the family of all Tathāgatas, one shall be born in the Pure Land;

third, one should not do so for the sake of escaping the suffering of illness, but rather vow that for the sake of healing the sores of ignorance and the like within all worlds, one shall be born in the Pure Land; fourth, one should not do so for the sake of becoming a wheel-turning monarch.
Therefore, the first vow is to turn the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, to act as a Great Dharma King, and to be born in the Pure Land;
fifth, not for the sake of the desire realm, the vow is to leave behind all subtle and exquisite five desires and to be born in the Pure Land;
sixth, not for the sake of the form realm, the vow is to leave behind all attachment to dhyāna and to be born in the Pure Land; seventh, not for the sake of...

Because it pertains to the formless realm, every aspiration is for the exhaustion of all various subtle streams [of existence], so as to realize a body endowed with immeasurable marks and signs and be born in a pure land;

eighth, because it is not for the sake of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, every aspiration is to benefit all sentient beings through the two adornments of merit and wisdom, so as to be born in a pure land;
ninth, because it is not for the sake of a single world-system or a thousand world-systems...
May each and every vow replace the suffering of beings throughout incalculable worlds, so that all beings in all worlds may be uprooted from suffering and born into the Pure Land;
tenth, for the sake of beings throughout one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* and a thousand *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*,
may each and every vow replace the suffering of immeasurable and innumerable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* beings, so that all beings may be uprooted from suffering and born into the Pure Land.
If one can thus give rise to such great vows, then at the final moment, one will certainly be as described in the Vows of Samantabhadra;
therefore, one should know that vows are the vessel for crossing the ocean of suffering and the enlightened teacher who guides one to Sukhāvatī.
Regarding the sevenfold pure precepts: all pure dharmas take the precepts as their foundation.
It is like a person building a house who first seeks level ground, or a painter who first prepares the bright, smooth canvas before applying colors; the precepts are likewise.
Therefore, the precepts are the foremost of all wholesome dharmas and the initial gateway for entering a pure land. If one does not uphold the precepts, [one cannot enter].
Just as it is impossible for a woman defiled by impurities to enter a ritual altar, so too is it impossible [for one who lacks these qualities].
First, the precept of non-avarice, which means practicing the two kinds of giving—of wealth and life—as well as the giving of the Dharma, because there is no stinginess.

Second, the precept of not violating prohibitions, which means fully maintaining the five precepts, the rules of discipline (*vinaya*), and even up to the untainted (*anāsrava*) precepts. Third, the precept of freedom from anger, which means disciplining the mind through patience.

Furthermore, regarding the body and speech, if one encounters harsh words or is struck by blades and staves, one should simply contemplate the law of karmic causes and conditions, maintaining the thought that this is a debt being repaid, the thought that one is a guide, and the thought that it is like the sensations of wind, cold, and heat. Thus, there are four precepts against negligence:
in the perilous paths of birth and death, there is no place for physical laxity; it is like a person carrying a bowl full of oil walking along a suspended rope, unable to look left or right.

5. The precept of non-distraction: because it involves observing until the second thought arises, it consists of guarding and collecting the sense faculties and stilling the shadows of external conditions;
it is like protecting a lamp from the wind or warding off a bird about to hatch its eggs. 6. The precept of non-delusion: because it uses wisdom to shatter all confusion and bewilderment;
it is like a laborer who must always rely on the sunlight, for if it were a long night, all work would be abandoned. Furthermore, it is like...
Ascending and viewing [the heights] should serve to open one's eyes; if one were blind or asleep, the mountains, rivers, and great earth would be no different from nothingness.

Seventh is the precept against pride: one should not be haughty on account of one’s eloquence, nor haughty on account of one’s realization and understanding, nor haughty on account of one’s debating skills; all that is attained is like [a mere speck] upon the great earth.
8. The precept against concealing faults: Just as dust is like grime on the surface of a mirror, one should not take pride in this grime because of that very grime;
for in all places, the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and the divine spirits are everywhere present, and there is nothing that can be concealed.
It is like trying to escape a shadow in the sunlight, moisture in water, or dust in sand—there is nowhere to hide. 9. The precept against useless conduct.
That is to say, one should distance oneself from all matters of frivolous play, which are of no benefit; all poetry and prose, which are of no benefit;

all worldly attachments, which are of no benefit; and all verbal liberation, which is of no benefit. The ten precepts of non-abiding refer to the aforementioned observance of the precepts solely for the purpose of being born in a pure land and benefiting sentient beings, without seeking fame, reputation, the Dharma, or the states of humans, devas, or the two vehicles.
Because it is the fruit [of their practice], when Bodhisattvas thus practice pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), they are able to gather all sentient beings and cause them to be born in a Pure Land.
Why is this? Although all sentient beings may be as stubborn and dull-witted as possible, there are none who do not hold the virtue of ethical discipline in profound reverence.
Regarding the eight pure abodes: a practitioner of the Way who has already resolved to transcend the mundane world ought to abandon all unwholesome places.

If one does not abandon them, it must be that their revulsion and detachment have not reached their ultimate limit. If revulsion and detachment have not reached their ultimate limit, it must be that their aspiration for the Pure Land has not reached its ultimate limit.
Nāgārjuna said: "The mind of a Bodhisattva does not prize the status of a Cakravartin King or the blessings and pleasures of humans and devas; rather, they contemplate only..."

For this reason, the Buddhas manifest in Buddha-lands according to what the mind values; if one cannot even relinquish a small place that brings momentary pleasure, how much less so the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King?
Like one whose feet are bound while wishing to walk, or whose wings are tethered while seeking to fly—whether staying or going, both are burdens.
First, one should distance oneself from places of empty entanglement and bustling luxury; second, from places of singing pavilions and wine shops.

One should stay far away from the three places scorched by the flames of fever; one should stay far away from the four places where discursive arguments regarding worldly affairs and court matters arise;
one should stay far away from the six places where one is entangled by the bonds of affection and where one has long roamed and frequented;

one should stay far away from the seven places of poetic assemblies and literary societies where verses are contended for and lines are scrutinized; and one should stay far away from the places where the ancient and modern are satirized and length and brevity are compared.

One should stay far away from these for ten reasons: first, because they lack the flavor of the Dharma; second, because they are devoid of the essence of the Path; third, because they are merely the pursuit of fame and profit; fourth, because they involve the recitation of mantras and incantations;

fifth, because they concern the study of worldly arts and crafts; sixth, because they involve the recitation of secular books; seventh, because they are places where those who preach heterodox doctrines gather;

eighth, because they are places where scholars of the meaning and doctrine engage in disputes over names and characteristics and prize petty wisdom; ninth, because they are places where those with deluded understandings of the fundamental vehicle talk wildly of sudden enlightenment while disparaging the precepts; and tenth, because such things disturb the Path and are no different from demons. Therefore, practitioners should stay far away from them.
If one is separated from these various bases, all the tasks of the path will be accomplished.
Regarding the nine types of pure companions: the capacity for all awakening does not arise without a friend, and all unwholesome dharmas do not cease without a friend;
it is like the two wheels of a chariot—if one is missing, one stumbles. Therefore, even the worldly methods of letters and conceptual proliferation must still...

How much more so for those whose minds are unified and who aspire to the causes and conditions of the unsurpassed Great Way! As the *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Seeking the Unsurpassed Great Way* states:
"For example, although the nature of wind is empty, when it blows from a grove of sandalwood or a grove of campaka flowers, the wind carries a wondrous fragrance;

yet if it passes through excrement, filth, or a putrid corpse, that wind becomes foul-smelling. It is also like a clean garment placed inside a fragrant casket: when the garment is taken out, it retains the scent of the fragrance."

If incense is placed in a foul place, the clothing also becomes foul; friends are likewise so. Therefore, one who practices the Way and seeks friends should strictly distinguish between the pure and the defiled:
first, one should stay close to friends who are at home in mountain forests, for they can quell a restless mind;
second, one should stay close to friends who strictly uphold the precepts, for they can subdue all desires; third, [one should stay close to] friends whose wisdom is vast and great.

1. One should associate with the friend of the four *dhāraṇīs*, for they enable one to emerge from the marshes of delusion; 2. One should associate with the friend of letters, for they enable one to resolve doubts and difficulties; 3.
One should associate with the friend of solitude and austerity, for they enable one to remain tranquil while making progress;

4. One should associate with the friend of humility and patience, for they enable one to eliminate pride and self-importance; 5. One should associate with the friend of upright mind and loyal admonition, for they enable one to restrain [unwholesome thoughts].

Because of these various faults, one should associate with eight types of friends: (1) those who are courageous and diligent in their spiritual efforts, for they can swiftly lead one to the fruits of the Path;
(2) those who regard wealth lightly and delight in giving, for they can break through excessive stinginess;

(3) those who are compassionate and protect all beings, not sparing even their own bodies or lives, for they can destroy the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self. If such pure companions are absent, one should instead remain in seclusion.
When a person dwells alone, they should personally cultivate the path and take the images of the Buddhas as their teacher and the sūtras and śāstras as their companions;

as for those who indulge in frivolous play, one should sever all contact with them rather than communicate. This is because, just as in a garden where there may be no fine flowers, one should not plant foul-smelling weeds, as they do nothing to benefit the aesthetic mind and only serve to increase loathing and impurity.
Regarding the ten indeterminate purities: the faculties of all sentient beings differ in being either sharp or dull.
As for the aforementioned dharmas, it is only those with superior faculties and sharp instruments who can fully attain them.

Therefore, the Tathāgata employs diverse skillful means to open the gates of the nine grades, dividing them into superior, middling, and inferior, and cultivating three levels of practice. The first is when one understands the meaning of the truths but has not yet fully subdued the afflictions.
First, because they do not deeply understand [the meaning] but are merely able to recite and read the various sutras;
second, because they produce faith based merely on the words, or produce faith due to others, or produce faith upon encountering poverty and humiliation;

third, because they contemplate a golden image, or contemplate a single mark according to their preference; fourth, because they perform ten recitations, a hundred recitations, or even a thousand recitations in the early morning.
Fifth, some may merely repent of their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) and the ten unwholesome karmas;

sixth, some may resolve to be reborn there out of fear of birth and death, or resolve to be reborn there upon encountering suffering and hardship, provided they do not make aspirations for the realms of humans or devas, nor for various merits and blessings;
seventh, some may merely observe the eight precepts, the five precepts, or even just the basic moral precepts.

Eighth, because one has abandoned killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, one cannot suddenly leave all noisy and distracting environments, yet from time to time one gives rise to a mind of weary detachment (*nirveda*).
Ninth, regarding worldly dharmas, one cannot immediately sever attachment to them, but one does not comply with or follow after them.
Tenth, as explained in the "Lower Grades" section of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, it may be through merely ten recitations at the moment of death. These are the aforementioned dharmas.
Those who can, with a sincere heart, receive and uphold even a single dharma shall all attain rebirth; however, they must not allow doubt and faith to intermingle.
If one harbors doubt, all spiritual practices will fail to achieve fulfillment. It is like a person walking alone on a distant road at night who must not entertain doubt.
Therefore, for sentient beings, hearing the Dharma and doubting it is not as good as not hearing it at all. Why is this? Because...
Those who have not heard [the Dharma] simply have not heard it because there were no obstacles; this [latter case], however, is because they themselves created the obstacles.
*Xi-fang-he-lun*, Scroll Nine.
*Xi-fang-he-lun*, Scroll Ten.
Tenth: Explaining Alternative Classifications.
Now, the general principles of the West are clearly elucidated within the sutras themselves, while the essential gates of the Pure Land are fully explained in various treatises.
Masters such as Vasubandhu, Zhiyi, the masters of Goryeo (Haedong), and Yuexi have all probed the profound subtleties and extolled the core tenets; more recently, Yunqi [Lianchi] has done the same.

The commentaries and sub-commentaries composed by the Upādhyāya categorize and analyze the texts with such precision, profundity, and vastness that they truly serve as a long torch to illuminate the night’s path and a light boat to cut across the sea of suffering.

Although there is nothing further to be revealed regarding the teachings already set forth by the various masters, there remain occasional differences in the timing of the establishment of doctrines and the exposition of meanings within the various sūtras; these differences give rise to doubt and apprehension among students. Now...
I have briefly extracted [these points] from various treatises and appended my own observations, synthesizing them into a single location for the sake of reference. This consists of:
(1) an explanation of the distance of the buddha-fields; (2) an explanation of the size of the city of the two bodies;
(3) an explanation of the duration of the lifespan; and (4) an explanation of the size of the flower-wheels.
5. Explanation of the existence or non-existence of the moon on the fifteenth day; 6. Explanation of the existence or non-existence of the two vehicles;
7. Explanation of the existence or non-existence of women; 8. Explanation of the greatness or smallness of the resolve for enlightenment;
9. Explanation of the city of doubt and birth from a womb; 15. Explanation of the rebirth of those who have committed the five heinous crimes.

Regarding the distance of one *kṣetra*: various major and minor sūtras all state that the West is ten thousand *koṭi* of *kṣetras* from here, yet the *Amitābha Sūtra* alone states that Amitābha Buddha is not far from here.
Which of these two accounts is correct? The explanation is that because distance is not fixed, it is said to be both far and near.
Why is this so? Generally speaking, when one speaks of a certain direction, that direction reaches [the destination].
To say that one direction reaches another through so many cities and lands is to establish the characteristics of a body based on a physical form;
since such a body is empty, the directions and distances thus calculated are likewise unreal. One cannot therefore say who is near or who is far.

It is like the person from Yunnan claiming that the land of Yan is distant—this is because they calculate it from Yunnan, yet for Yan itself, there is no such distance. It is as the person from Qi says regarding the land of Yan.
"Nearness" is established based on calculation; therefore, in reality, Yan is not near Qi. It is like ten paces of ground:
for an ant it is distant, but for an elephant it is near. One should not say that "distance" is real. Why? Because this ground should not be calculated from the perspective of the ant.

Nor should one say that "nearness" is real. Why? Because this ground should not be calculated from the perspective of the elephant. Furthermore, consider the calculation: [the same applies to]... (further elaboration follows)."
That which is ten paces away is also not real. Why? Because this ground does not originate from the ant, nor from the elephant, nor is it appropriate to calculate it based on the person;
therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "It is spoken of as having directions in accordance with what is transmitted by worldly convention;
yet direction is ultimately unobtainable. Question: Why do you say there is no direction? Is this direction both existent and eternal, as stated in the sūtras?
Where the sun rises is the East; where the sun sets is the West; where the sun travels is the South; and where the sun does not travel is the North.
The sun has three divisions of conjunction: if it conjoins with the front [the East], if it conjoins with the present [the South], or if it conjoins with the rear [the West].
Whichever direction the solar division first conjoins with, that is the East; the South and West are likewise. Where the sun does not travel is [the North].
Without a portion [of the sun], he replied: "It is not so. Mount Sumeru stands in the midst of the four continents.

As the sun revolves around Mount Sumeru, it illuminates the four worlds under heaven. When it is midday in Uttarakuru (i.e., the Northern Kuru Continent), the sun rises over Pūrvavideha (i.e., the Eastern Godānīya Continent).
The people of Pūrvavideha are in the east; when it is midday there, the sun rises over Jambudvīpa. The people of Jambudvīpa are in the east."
In this way, space is truly without beginning. Why? Because all directions are equally the east, equally the south, equally the west, and equally the north.

Your claim that the place where the sun rises is the east, the place where the sun travels is the south, the place where the sun sets is the west, and the place where the sun does not travel is the north, is incorrect. [The opponent] asks: "I am speaking of a single country."
The Master said: "I consider the four directions to be difficult to establish for this reason: the eastern direction is not without a beginning. He replied:
"If in one country the sun conjoins with the east, then that [east] has a limit. Because it has a limit, it is impermanent; because it is impermanent, it is not all-pervading.
For this reason, there is only the name 'direction' but no reality. Thus, even the concept of spatial location cannot be established."
How could there be a fixed course for its attainment? Nevertheless, it does not discard spatial location or a course. Why is this?

Because while one should not calculate it according to Jambudvīpa, it can also be calculated according to Jambudvīpa. This is just as the sun, although it neither truly rises in the east nor sets in the west, may nevertheless be said to rise in the east and set in the west.
Regarding the dimensions of the two cities of the body: the *Śrīkūṭarāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states that Amitābha Buddha dwells together with his śrāvakas in a land called Qingtai (Pure Peace);
the city where the Holy King resides is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
The *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* states that the Buddha’s body is sixty million billion nayuta Ganges-sands of yojanas in height, and between his eyebrows is a white tuft of hair curling to the right.
The swirling and revolving [halo] is like five Mount Sumerus; the Buddha-eye is like the waters of the four great oceans.

Calculating one ocean at eighty-four thousand *yojanas*, the four oceans together total three hundred thirty-six thousand *yojanas*. His body exceeds his eye by five million six hundred thousand *yojanas*;
even calculating the city where he dwells, it is still less than the eye by three hundred twenty-two thousand six hundred [yojanas].
If [the distance between] the cities is a thousand *yojanas*, how much more so for his body? It should not be that the body and the city are so vastly separated.
This question also appears in the *Shixianghai Dongshu* (Eastern Commentary on the Ocean of Meanings). The commentary states: "That Buddha has many cities;

according to the size of the assembly, the cities are also large or small. Within the large cities, he manifests a great body; within the small cities, he appears with a small body. The *Śrīghoṣarāja Sūtra* says:
One should know that the city where he dwells together with the śrāvakas measures ten thousand yojanas; it corresponds in scale to the body of the Buddha.

One should understand that the great height and magnitude described in the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Buddha* (Kuan-fo san-mei hai ching) indicate that the city is likewise vast, as it is the place where great assemblies of followers dwell together.
As the former masters have said: "In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Pure Radiance Adorned Land (*Vimalaprabhā-vyūha*) expounds only the sudden teaching."
In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, because the Buddha-land of Universal Fragrance consists exclusively of bodhisattvas, that Buddha manifests only a body of great height and majesty.

In contrast, because in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) both sudden and gradual teachings are expounded, and śrāvakas and bodhisattvas together constitute the Saṃgha, the Buddha displays two types of manifestations:

the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*). The thirty-two marks are common to both the birth-body and the dharma-body, as they pertain to both the Great and the Small Vehicles.
As for the vision of the eighty thousand marks, these are restricted to the Dharmakāya and are perceived only by the noble ones of the Mahāyāna.

Therefore, for those who are to obtain the four benefits through the *cangchen* (藏塵) marks of the *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa* (尊特), the Buddha manifests the *cangchen* *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa* body in accordance with their capacity;
for those who are to obtain the four benefits through the eighty thousand *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*, the Buddha manifests the eighty thousand [marks] in accordance with their capacity.
Regarding the "Exalted Unique Body" (vairocanakāya), one should understand that it is attained through the thirty-two marks of the Exalted Unique Body which yield four benefits.

When the Buddha manifests the body of the thirty-two marks of the Exalted Unique Body in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings—just as Vairocana does—the śrāvakas’ vision and hearing are obstructed by their inability to face him directly;

yet this does not prevent bodhisattvas from seeing his even greater body. Why is this? Because the Buddha’s body appears large or small according to the capacity of those it reaches, just like the sun.
Just as light follows a crack, appearing large or small depending on the opening, yet the sunlight itself has no such dimensions;

thirdly, regarding the length of their lifespans, the Sūtra states that the life of that Buddha is immeasurable and boundless, spanning incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and further states that when that Buddha reaches *parinirvāṇa*, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva shall then become a Buddha. Since this is so...

"Entering extinction is precisely having a limit" (these two phrases constitute the scriptural text posing a challenge). A former master explained: "The *bhūmi-pratipannaka* (candidate for Buddhahood) of the *pitaka* and *tong* teachings (referring to the *bhūmi-pratipannaka* bodhisattvas taught in the *pitaka* and *tong* vehicles) manifests that the Buddha has limits;

the *bhūmi-pratipannaka* of the *bie* and *yuan* teachings reveals that the Buddha is limitless. (This clarifies the aforementioned meaning of the Buddha being limitless): because all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods of time have no distinction between self and other and do not see one another, they share the same *dharmakāya* and the same wisdom;

thus, the bodhisattva’s capacity for perception ceases (a portion of ignorance is exhausted), and the Tathāgata’s response-activity subsides (the traces of his responsive transformations cease); this is called [the state of]...

In the *Supplement to the Buddha’s Place* (*Bùfóchù*), it is stated that the Real [Body] is truly distinct from the previous Buddhas of the Shared and Distinct Teachings, because the former Buddhas have definitely entered extinction while the latter Buddhas have definitely arisen.
Thus, the *Commentary on the Four Buddhas Descending into the Chamber of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* explains:

"If one sees the four Buddhas as having the same *Mahāpuruṣa* body, with one body and one wisdom, this is the Eternal Body, for the assembly of disciples is one. If one sees the four Buddhas as having different Buddha-bodies, this is the Responsive [Body]."

Because the transformed disciples are so numerous (their multitude being exceedingly vast), [these several phrases conclude by clarifying that] the doctrines of identity, difference, unity, and multiplicity are all non-existent. Therefore, one knows that the body of the entire Dharma-realm is neither born nor extinguished;

how could it be divided vertically into past and present, or discussed horizontally in terms of self and other? Since it is neither born nor extinguished, the meaning of the immeasurable is established.

Furthermore, within the pure Buddha-lands, even the lands as numerous as motes of dust, the waters, and the trees are all the Buddha-body; thus, the sutra says: "All these various birds are all Amitābha."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Sentient beings are exceedingly numerous. If the Buddha were to manifest his body in every place, sentient beings would not believe it, regarding it as a magical illusion;

their minds would lack reverence. Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, when hearing the Dharma from a human, do not attain awakening, yet if they hear the Dharma from an animal, they immediately believe and accept it—as described in the *Jātaka-sūtra* regarding the Bodhisattva’s births.
When one in the form of an animal preaches the Dharma to humans, because such preaching of the Dharma is so rare, there are none who do not believe and accept it.
Some say that animals are sentient beings, and since even trees, which lack consciousness, can produce sounds, all believe and accept this.
For this reason, water, trees, and birds are all manifestations of the Buddha’s body. Thus, if the lifespan of the Buddha were...
If that which is exhausted were the Bodhimanda, the buddha-fields, and the sounds of the water birds, then these too would have an end.

If they had an end, there could be no succession [of Buddhas]; if they had no end, one should not speak of their cessation. (If the fields, the water birds, and so forth were all exhausted, how then could there be a place for succession? These four lines correspond to the scriptural passage cited at the beginning.
Like the limits of space, they are neither possessed of limits nor devoid of limits; they can be apprehended by means of inconceivable wisdom.
Regarding the large and small sizes of the four flower-wheels: the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra in Eight Thousand Lines* states that the lotuses in the ponds are as large as chariot wheels.

The *Amitābha Sūtra* (Kuan-ching) says that within each pond there are sixty billion lotuses made of the seven precious gems, perfectly round (meaning their circumference) and exactly twelve yojanas in size.
The *Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that the lotuses in the ponds are either one yojana, up to a hundred yojanas, or even a thousand yojanas in size.
The human world’s chariot wheel does not exceed ten feet in diameter; even the golden thousand-spoked wheel of a Cakravartin King is no more than one yojana in length and breadth.

How can there be such a vast disparity between their sizes? The Buddha explained that the size of the lotus wheels is likewise according to the body-cities [of the beings], for because the capacities of sentient beings vary in size, the body-cities, waters, trees, and lotus flowers appear accordingly in different sizes.

Just as in the first bhūmi, one transforms a hundred buddha-fields (meaning that those transformed by a bodhisattva of the first bhūmi number a hundred buddha-fields), and sees a hundred-petaled flower; in the second bhūmi, one transforms a thousand buddha-fields and sees a thousand-petaled flower;

in the third, ten thousand petals; in the fourth, one hundred million petals; in the fifth, one thousand billion petals; in the sixth, one hundred thousand billion petals; in the seventh, one hundred thousand billion nayutas of petals;
and in the eighth, petals equal in number to the atoms within a hundred thousand million three-thousandfold world systems.
The number [of lands] is equal to the atoms in nine *bhūmis* of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* worlds;
the number [of Buddhas] is equal to the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayutas* of Buddhas in the tenth *bhūmi*.

Because the self-enjoyment bodies (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) have varying sizes, the visions of the flowers are likewise so; it is not that the flowers themselves have varying sizes. I have often heard monks say that on the seashore there was an Aśoka.
When sentient beings behold the King’s Śarīra stūpa, the manifestations of its radiance differ for each: some see it as being without light;
some see light the size of a small bean; some see it like a jujube fruit; some see it as large as the tip of a finger; and some see it as large as a peck-measure (*dōu*).

Even among those who see it as large as a peck-measure, not even one in a thousand sees it the same way. Thus, although sentient beings possess the same physical eyes, what they perceive still differs.
How much more so for Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and even humans and devas—their spiritual efforts are vastly different; how could the flower-wheels they manifest not differ?

In this land, noble Kṣatriya lineages abound with soaring towers and magnificent pavilions filling the cities, while those of humble or orphaned status dwell in huts of withered thatch or earthen caves; it would be difficult to argue otherwise regarding such vast disparities in scale.
For what reason is it that this is summoned by one's own merit? Thus, the association with the flowers of the jewel-pool is likewise.

Regarding whether the sun and moon exist or not: various editions either state that the sun and moon abide in space, or state that they abide in space but do not circulate, or do not mention their existence or non-existence, or simply state that they do not exist at all. Furthermore, a sutra says: "The light of that Buddha is universal..."
The Buddha-fields are illuminated by immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable radiance that eclipses the sun and moon.

All the assembly of śrāvakas possess bodily light capable of illuminating a fathom; the light of the bodhisattvas extends for hundreds of thousands of fathoms. The two bodhisattvas (Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta) constantly illuminate the trichiliocosm with their radiance.
Thus, although the sun and moon exist there, they are like torches in the presence of a great fire.
How could the sun possess light that illuminates like the sun and moon? If it were unable to illuminate, there would be no day or night.
Why, then, does the Sūtra speak of the six periods of day and night, as well as matters such as the time for the morning meal? It is clear that these are also expedient teachings;

they borrow the metaphor of day and night to illustrate those temporal divisions and do not refer to actual entities. Furthermore, the coming and going of day and night is but the mind of sentient beings.
Because the perception of such phenomena arises from the mutual influence of light and darkness, a pure buddha-field should not possess these features.
Even in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which is already above [the earth], one does not depend on the sun and moon; how much more so in the Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī)?

Even if they were present there, it would be because the sentient beings of that transformed land have not yet exhausted their views regarding form and emptiness, and thus perceive the appearance of such a sun and moon; in reality, however, the Buddha-land is devoid of them.

There are no [lands] without suns and moons; as stated in the *Mahā-śāstra*, Śākyamuni Buddha has other pure lands like those of Amitābha Buddha, and Amitābha Buddha likewise has impure lands like those of Śākyamuni Buddha.
These are taught according to the perceptions and capacities of sentient beings, and thus there is no contradiction in asserting that such lands exist.
Regarding the existence or non-existence of the two vehicles (the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* vehicles), one asks the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra-ṭīkā* by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu:

"In the realm of the roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna, there are no names even to be censured, and so forth, until one does not even hear the name of the two vehicles, let alone their actual existence. [This implies that] in the Western Land, which is the realm of the roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna, there are no names of the two vehicles that could be subject to censure.
Yet, in all these sūtras, it is stated that the śrāvakas in that land are beyond measure; for what reason, then, do the former masters explain that the two vehicles are born there?

These individuals are all those who, at the time of death, turn from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle; because their practice of the Small has been profound, they hear what the Buddha teaches, and even the sounds of wind in the branches and water resonate as the Small.
Thus, they temporarily realize the fruits of the Small, yet gradually advance until they reach the stage of a Bodhisattva. It is not that they remain in the Small;
therefore, it is said that there are no two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*). There are two meanings to this: first, that the Two Vehicles are not fixed [in their status].
Because birth is truly non-existent, these two do not abide; because the Two Vehicles are ultimately non-existent, they are like two officials serving together in the same ministry:
one official’s tenure ends here, while the other is about to be promoted. The one whose tenure has ended may still be called an "official" because he lacks a subsequent office;
however, the one who is about to be promoted is not definitively an "official," for his status as an official will ultimately change.
For this reason, it cannot be said that there are two vehicles (dviyāna) in the Pure Land, because one ultimately reaches the stage of a Bodhisattva.
Regarding the presence or absence of women: in the *Śrī-rāja-sūtra*, it is stated that Amitābha Buddha also had parents;

how then can it be said that there are no women? This [land] is also a transformation, like a transformed parrot. The *Haedong-so* (Commentary from the East of the Sea) states: "The *Ghoṣarāja-sūtra*..."
It is taught that the Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Peace and Bliss has parents who are transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) and not bodies of actual retribution (*vipāka-kāya*).
Furthermore, although he has parents, they do not give birth through the womb; he is truly born by transformation (*upapāduka*), and his parents are merely assumed for the sake of expediency.
As that sūtra says: "If the fourfold assembly can correctly receive [the name of the Buddha]—meaning they maintain it with right mindfulness—and by this merit, when their lives come to an end..."
At that time, Amitābha Buddha immediately arises amidst the great assembly and causes them to dwell at this person’s location, enabling them to see him.

Having seen him, their joy increases manifold and their merit grows. By virtue of these causes and conditions, wherever they are born, they will forever be free from the defiled forms of the womb and desire;
they will be born spontaneously within fresh and wondrous precious lotus flowers, endowed with great supernormal powers and radiant, brilliant light.
Yi, you should know that parents are merely a temporary lodging. Some claim that the *Śabdavajra-sūtra* states there are parents;

this is intended to show that the Buddha resides in a defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra*). This interpretation is incorrect. Why? Because that sūtra also states that [the Buddha] is born by transformation from a precious lotus and that two bodhisattvas stand in attendance at his left and right;
all such features are characteristics of a pure land (*śuddha-kṣetra*) and are no different from what is seen in the *Avalokiteśvara-vyūha*.
Because it is so stated in the sūtras, one should know that those [beings] such as Devadatta and Māra mentioned in the sūtras are all manifestations produced within the Pure Land;
they do not exist there because these individuals render it an impure land, for the manifestation of animals does not make a land defiled.
Regarding the eight types of generating the mind [of enlightenment] and their relative magnitude: among the three grades in the Wei translation, all involve generating the bodhicitta;

whereas in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, the lowest grade speaks directly of "ten recitations. Since these various sūtras differ, if one wishes to harmonize them, one must recognize that in all sūtras, it is the generation of the great bodhicitta that serves as the cause.
Why is this? Because if one lacks the great cause at the very outset, such a person— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Even though these teachings have passed through one's ears, doubts and difficulties may still arise as to how they can be heard and believed all at once.
Therefore, one should know that those who possess even ten moments of inferior mindfulness (*daśa-nimitta*) must have planted great causes in previous lives;

subsequently, having fallen back, they encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) at the time of death, just as a sprout in a drought receives rain and suddenly bursts forth from its sheath. If there were no such prior cause, one would not even be able to meet a virtuous friend.
How much more so for those who encounter it and believe and accept it! There are many among the wise and the nobility who become increasingly incredulous the more they hear;

thus one knows that hearing it once and immediately bringing it to mind is no small cause. One should not, because a person has committed evil in this life, conclude that they lack great causes [for liberation].
As the Sūtra says: "If the people of the world hear the name of Amitābha and [respond with] compassion..."

Those whose hearts are filled with joy, whose hair stands on end, and from whom tears immediately flow, have all practiced the Buddha-way over successive lifetimes, or have served as bodhisattvas under other Buddhas in other realms.

For this reason, whether one is dull-witted or wise, anyone who recollects the Buddha with a sincere heart has planted the roots of goodness deeply over many kalpas and has given rise to the great mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta). Why is this so? It is because:
Roots of goodness do not refer exclusively to wisdom; yet if one lacks these roots, it is like a scorched seed—how could any sprout emerge?

In this world, even regarding the minor art of chess, there are those of lowly and ignorant status who master it instantly and become proficient at once, while a man of intelligence may practice it for a lifetime and remain at the bottom of the ranks.
One should know that this is because the skill is minor; without the necessary causes, one cannot even enter its depths.
How much more so for the Great Dharma! Therefore, if there is anyone who has faith in this rare and difficult-to-believe teaching, that person is indeed a bodhisattva of great resolve.
Thus, those born from the womb in the City of Nine Doubts—the Yuan-Wei translation states: "If there are sentient beings who fall into doubt and regret and accumulate [karmic seeds]..."
Regarding their roots of goodness— the aspiration for the Buddha’s wisdom, universal wisdom, inconceivable wisdom, unequaled wisdom, majestic and virtuous wisdom, and vast wisdom—
they were unable to give rise to faith in those roots of goodness themselves; yet, because they gave rise to faith upon hearing the name of the Buddha,

by virtue of this causal condition, for five hundred years they remained within a flower-womb, perceiving it as nothing more than a pleasure grove, a palace, or a celestial mansion, and did not see [the physical form].
Not hearing the Buddha’s Dharma is called "womb-birth" (the Wei translation says: "failing to understand the Buddha's wisdom").
Nevertheless, they believe in sin and merit, cultivate the roots of goodness, and vow to be born in that land; for this reason, it is called womb-birth. The Song translation says:

"The roots of goodness planted by sentient beings cannot transcend [dualistic] marks; they do not seek the Buddha’s wisdom but falsely give rise to discrimination, being deeply attached to worldly pleasures and human blessings."

As a reward for this, the *Wangshi ben* (Original Text of the Wang Family) states: "If there are sentient beings who cultivate various merits and vow to be born in that land, yet later harbor doubts and regrets,
disbelieving in the existence of that Buddha-land and disbelieving that performing good deeds brings merit— though such persons may act thus, if they continue to maintain a mindful heart,
alternating between brief moments of faith and lack thereof, the Buddha will manifest his body before them at the time of their death."
Because they cause those beings to see with their own eyes and repent with their minds, their transgressions are diminished and they are born in that land; this is called "womb-birth" (*garbhaja*).
Now, according to the previous two translations, those who do not believe in the self-nature [of reality] and do not understand the Buddha’s wisdom are termed "womb-born.
Thus, the Song translation states directly that those who cultivate good deeds to seek birth among humans or devas are womb-born; in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), there is no womb-birth.

Therefore, as for the Wang family, they further hold that those who do not believe in the Buddha-fields, do not believe in sin and merit, and have only fleeting belief and fleeting disbelief, are "womb-born" (tāi-sheng) and differ from the two types of rebirth previously mentioned in the translations—namely, rebirth through hearing the name and giving rise to faith, and rebirth through the cultivation of the roots of goodness.
Generally speaking, the Pure Land is said to have nine grades; if explained in detail, there are ten million grades, which cannot be fully exhausted even now.
Those born among humans possess various karmic rewards for their merits and various karmic retributions for their transgressions, each being distinct.
Therefore, although the various translations differ from one another, they are all words of truth. Among them, the translation by the Northern Wei is particularly profound in its underlying intent:

those who do not believe in their own roots of goodness rely on others to generate faith, which constitutes the City of Doubt; those who believe in their own fruits of goodness immediately realize [the truth] themselves.

The mind cannot attain entry into awakening through others; only by attaining awakening itself can one be liberated from doubt. Therefore, practicing while remaining unawakened ultimately remains separated from the womb of doubt.

"Womb" (garbha) has the meaning of enveloping and obscuring. For those who are unawakened, the various hindrances have not been thoroughly penetrated, and thus they are destined to receive such retribution.

These individuals should be categorized as belonging to the middle-lower, lower-middle, and lower-lower grades. Why? Because the latter two types of the lower grade (referring to the lower-middle and lower-lower) must pass through six [stages].
It takes twelve kalpas for the flower to bloom, yet this [person] has only five hundred years;

therefore, according to the *Wangben* (King’s Original Text), their faith in the Buddha is not as intense as that of the latter two types. Furthermore, since they are born in the borderlands of that land (i.e., a district or city), they should not be able to see the Buddha within five hundred years.

Regarding those who attain rebirth through the five grave offenses (*pañcānantarya*), the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Except for those who have committed the five grave offenses, slandered the True Dharma, or reviled the noble ones.
However, according to the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, even those who have committed the five grave offenses or the ten evil deeds may all attain rebirth through ten recitations at the time of death.
One should understand that the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* excludes those who commit the five grave offenses because of their slander; why? Because entry into the Pure Land is based on faith.
The slanderer of the Teacher is a thief of faith; just as water has nothing it cannot contain, yet it cannot contain fire because fire cannot be contained by it;

and just as wind has nowhere it does not enter, yet it does not enter stone because the stone itself cannot be penetrated—so too, those who slander burn the True Dharma like a fierce flame and obstruct the Buddha’s wisdom like an iron wall. Therefore:

The wind of wisdom from the ocean of Dharma can receive [the benefits of] the *Sūtra on the Contemplation of Amitāyus* without cause; the principle that it does not exclude those who commit the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) while excluding those who slander [the teaching] is identical in meaning though different in wording.
This is because although the five heinous crimes are extremely evil, they do not necessarily entail a view of absolute disbelief, and thus [such persons] should not be excluded.

However, there may be those of great resolve who initially do not believe, but later, through being inspired, they undergo a sudden awakening and repent of their former faults, such as [the case of] Han [Minju].

When Changli first denounced the Buddha-bone, he later took refuge with Dadian; Zhang Wujin initially reviled Buddhist scriptures, intending to compose a "Treatise on the Non-existence of the Buddha," but later, upon contemplating the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, he experienced profound awakening and ultimately became a dragon-elephant of the Chan school—this is truly a rare occurrence within the Dharma.
Therefore, among the eminent figures of the Confucian community, there may be those who, having heard erroneously or being influenced by prior misconceptions, have slandered [Buddhism].
In the Buddha-dharma, it is sufficient to swiftly seek reform and repentance; this itself is a magnificent achievement. One should not regard slander as an obstacle or hindrance.
*Xi-fang-he-lun* (The Comprehensive Treatise on the Western Regions), Volume Ten (End).
Postscript to the Annotations of *Xi-fang-he-lun*.
In the past, while I was traveling with Zhang Mingjiao (Wujiao) of Yingcheng to visit Master Yuan Zhonglang, he produced the *Western Regions Synthesis* (*Xifang helun*) for our inspection.
I was struck with wonder and admiration at how its synthesis of Chan and Pure Land surpassed all other scriptures concerning the Land of Bliss.
There were certain passages therein that I did not fully understand, so I requested to question the Master on them; he then instructed Mingjiao to provide annotations at the head of those sections.
When I brought [this text] back to the South and intended to carve it for the salvation of the world, I had not yet completed the task.
In the year Jǐwèi (1479), after the death of Qú Yuánchū (Chúnrén), a scholar of Hǎiyú, his bequeathed property was bestowed upon me.

I immediately consented to have ten volumes of the scripture carved before his spirit altar to dedicate them for his rebirth in the Pure Land. Recently, while recovering from an illness at Ruìguāng Temple in Wúmén, I recalled this previous commitment.
I pray that you will entrust this to Yuan Wuya (Shudu) to re-edit and collate it, and assign my disciple Xingcheng to oversee the task;
thus, on one hand, we shall repay Master Yuan’s grace for his Dharma-giving, and on the other, fulfill Mr. Qu’s aspiration for his material support.
As for the refinement of the composition and the excellence of the arguments, these must await the discernment of those with clear vision.
This is something you must realize for yourself; what more need I add?
Written on the day of the winter solstice in the month of Cháng during the first year of the Taichāng era of the Dàmíng period, the year of Gēngshēn, by the Elder Hèshí.
